📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I know, I know; poinsettias are absolutely the traditional choice for festive decorating, but there's another festive container plant that deserves a place by your front door this winter.

One of those underrated beauties that deserves its time in the spotlight, this holiday plant may not have the bold and colorful bracts of a classic poinsettia, but what it lacks in showy flowers, it more than makes up for in fragrance, evergreen foliage and year-round appeal.

In fact, if you're looking for a festive container plant that keeps on giving long after the holiday decorations have come down, it could be just the thing you're looking for (and then some!).

Industry observers note that poinsettias are practically synonymous with the holidays, and little wonder; their bright red, pink or white foliage brings an instant splash of festive color. Still, there's no getting away from the fact that their appeal is largely seasonal. They're tender plants, usually grown indoors in the US, and need warmth, bright indirect light, careful watering, and lots of TLC to keep them looking their best.

Sources indicate that once the holidays are over and those colorful bracts begin to fade, many poinsettias end up in the compost or trash. And, while it's possible to keep them growing and even encourage them to develop their colorful bracts again the following year, doing so takes a little effort.

Enter stage left, then, the beautiful sweet box (Sarcococca).

According to recent reports, obviously, sweet box offers a rather different proposition, as this handsome evergreen shrub doesn't have to be replaced when Christmas is over. In fact, its glossy leaves provide structure and greenery throughout the year, while its winter flowers bring a welcome surprise just when the garden can feel at its dullest.

According to recent reports, and it's not just about looks, either! Sweet box has a secret weapon that poinsettias simply can't compete with: its extraordinary perfume.

That's right, folks; sweet box produces masses of creamy-white flowers in winter, often tucked discreetly beneath its glossy leaves. They might not look particularly impressive from a distance, but get close and you'll discover why this shrub is so treasured, as they release a perfume often described as a combination of vanilla and jasmine.

Sources indicate that it's surprisingly powerful for such delicate blooms, and on a still winter day, the scent can drift through the garden and greet you as you approach your front door. Especially if you opt for a variety like the Sweet & Lo™ Sweet Box from Proven Winners.

Sources indicate that once flowering finishes, sweet box can produce ornamental berries, which mature from red to dark purple or black depending on the species and variety. And it does all of this while standing in partial or full shade, no less!

Recent findings suggest that although some sweet box varieties can eventually become quite substantial shrubs, its slow-growing nature also makes it a useful long-term container plant. (You won't be constantly battling to keep it in shape, for starters, although a light trim after flowering can help maintain a neat outline if needed).

Sources indicate that just be sure to choose a pot with drainage holes and use a good moisture-retentive potting mix. Pop it somewhere sheltered in partial or full shade, and water when the compost begins to dry – just like all container-grown plants, it will need a little more attention to watering than those growing in the ground, particularly during dry spells.

Of course, there's nothing wrong with a beautiful poinsettia, but if you'd rather invest in a plant that offers more than a few weeks of seasonal color, sweet box is well worth your time... not to mention a place in your heart. Not least of all because it's the sort of hard-working hero plant that continues to provide beauty long after the festive season has passed.

Sources indicate that if your home and garden is full of those awkward shady spots where other plants might struggle, then, look no further! And if not? Well, still show it some love, I say – for a festive container with fragrance, character and staying power, sweet box is a very hard plant to beat.

Sources indicate that halloween can be an exciting night for families, but all that activity can leave cats feeling unsettled. Strange costumes, unfamiliar visitors, and a doorbell that rings non-stop can be overwhelming, even for cats that usually enjoy meeting newly introduced people.

Industry observers note that the biggest concern is that a frightened cat may try to escape, while decorations, candy, and other seasonal hazards can create additional risks. A few simple changes around the home can help keep cats safe while everyone else enjoys the festivities.

Even households that don't celebrate Halloween can be affected by the extra noise and activity around the neighborhood. Excited children, unfamiliar costumes, barking dogs, loud music, and parties can create an unusually stressful environment for cats.

A frightened cat may bolt when strangers approach the house, and there's no guarantee it will head somewhere safe. A cat that escapes could become lost or run into traffic while trying to get away.

According to recent reports, keeping cats indoors is therefore one of the most notable Halloween precautions. Even cats that normally spend time outside should remain indoors, with windows and doors securely closed.

Industry observers note that with trick-or-treaters arriving throughout the evening, the front door may open far more often than usual. Every time it does, there's another opportunity for a cat to slip outside unnoticed.

Keeping a cat in a separate room when visitors arrive can reduce the risk, particularly if several people are coming and going. Making sure your cat is microchipped and that the registration details are up to date also improves the chances of being reunited if they do escape.

The simplest approach is to keep your cat away from the entrance for the entire evening rather than relying on everyone to remember to watch out for it.

Halloween decorations can look appealing to curious cats, but anything within reach may become a potential plaything. Curious cats can chew decorations or swallow small pieces, so it's best to avoid edible decorations and keep other items out of reach.

Carved pumpkins lit with real candles need particular care. A cat could knock one over, risking burns or even starting a fire.

Battery-operated candles offer a safer alternative. Another option is to place pumpkins outside or in a window where the cat can't reach them.

Recent findings suggest that it can be tempting to dress a cat up for Halloween, especially when everyone else in the household is wearing a costume. However, many cats find clothing uncomfortable or frightening, and restrictive outfits can cause unnecessary stress.

Some cats need to wear garments for medical reasons, such as a surgical vest to protect stitches after an operation. Halloween costumes are different because they generally serve no practical purpose for the cat.

Recent findings suggest that pay attention to how a cat responds to clothing and accessories. If they seem uncomfortable or distressed, leave the costume off. There are plenty of ways to include a cat in the celebration without dressing them up.

Candy presents several potential hazards for cats. Chocolate and certain other sweets contain ingredients that can be toxic to pets, while wrappers can become choking hazards if swallowed. Even sweets that aren't directly poisonous aren't suitable cat treats, and excess sugar can contribute to health problems.

Crinkly plastic wrappers can be particularly tempting because they appeal to a cat's instinct to chase and play with small objects. Itâs all fun and games when a cat bats them around, but they could end up swallowing them.

Recent findings suggest that keep Halloween treats in a closed container somewhere the cat can't access, and make sure children understand that sharing their candy with pets isn't safe. If a cat manages to eat candy, contact a vet promptly for advice.

Recent findings suggest that cats often cope with stress by hiding somewhere they feel safe. Providing a quiet room away from visitors and noise gives them the chance to retreat until the activity dies down.

A bedroom can work well, provided it has fresh water, a litter tray, and a favorite blanket or other familiar bedding. Guests should know that the room is off-limits so the cat isn't disturbed while resting.

Giving a cat this private space can be especially helpful during parties or evenings when the front door is opening repeatedly.

It has been revealed that it's sensible to check on a cat throughout Halloween, particularly when the household is busy. These checks help confirm that the cat is comfortable and hasn't slipped out unnoticed.

Recent findings suggest that however, checking in doesn't mean coaxing a frightened cat out of its hiding place. If they have chosen a quiet spot and appear settled, let them stay there.

The aim is to make sure the cat is safe without adding more attention or activity when it would rather be left alone.

Keeping a cat safe doesn't mean they have to be excluded from the evening entirely. Cats that dislike costumes can still feature in a Halloween photoshoot without wearing anything themselves. After all, theyâre already wearing the best outfit! Dressing as a character known for having a feline companion is another way to include a cat without making them uncomfortable.

A scary movie marathon can also be a relaxed way to spend the evening together. A soft, Halloween-themed blanket and a favorite treat might encourage a cat to settle on a lap, provided it enjoys that kind of attention.

Cat-friendly treats can be offered while the humans enjoy their own candy, and cats that like catnip may appreciate a Halloween-themed toy with a little dried catnip.

Halloween should be enjoyable for the whole household, but cats don't understand why the neighborhood suddenly becomes noisier or why strangers keep appearing at the door. Keeping them indoors, removing potential hazards, and providing somewhere quiet to retreat can make the night safer and more comfortable for everyone.

Sources indicate that fall-planted bulbs that flower in spring are surely the easiest, cheapest way to add color to your garden. Pop the bulbs into the ground in fall, then do absolutely nothing at all until green stems pierce the cold spring soil to light up your yard with fabulous flowers. From tulips to crocus, hyacinths to Dutch iris, there are plenty of showstopper bulbs you can still plant in November. As long as your ground isn’t frozen or waterlogged, all these beauties can be planted now, at a depth that's three times the bulb's height. If you live in a colder USDA zone and already past your first frost date, simply plant bulbs in a container in a sheltered spot instead.

When you’re planting bulbs in late fall, the secret to success is great drainage so they root rather than rot. That’s easily done by giving bulbs an inch-deep layer of grit to sit on at the base of the planting hole. You could fork out on horticultural grit, or you could simply use good ol’ poultry grit made of crushed granite like CZ Grain Chicken Grit, available from Walmart. You may need to protect tasty tulip bulbs from hungry squirrels, but then you can leave the rest to Mother Nature.

In a recent development, if it’s a while since you went bulb shopping, you’re in for a lovely surprise because plant breeders have been busy creating all sorts of wonderful fresh flower shapes and color combinations. From double-petalled tulips that look just like peonies to fragrant hyacinths in dramatic hues, these backyard blooms are a real springtime treat and planting them should be on everyone's list of gardening jobs in November. So let's skip straight to the good bit, shall we? Here’s my pick of dazzling spring-flowering bulbs to plant in late fall. Get the drainage right and all these will return year in, year out and with prices from 35 cents a bulb, there’s an option to suit every budget.

Sources indicate that looking at them, it was impossible to see a dog or cat as simply another expense. These animals were part of the family. They brought comfort, protection, affection, and, very often, a little joy into lives that could use more of it.

According to recent reports, that is something Julie and FoodBank Lakeside understand well. Helping someone feed their pet is not just about putting food in a bowl. It is about helping preserve a very notable relationship.

It has been revealed that as we moved from house to house, we also carried treats for the dogs we met along the way. They promptly learned that the cars arriving meant something good was coming.

Julie did not set out to create a large pet food program.

Local rescue groups were also concerned that families who could no longer afford to feed their dogs might eventually have to surrender them or turn them loose.

Sources indicate that julie started small. She bought large 25-kilogram bags of food, repackaged them herself, and drove into local communities to distribute them. As local groups organized despensas for families in villages around Lake Chapala, Julie saw an opportunity to make sure the pets were not forgotten. Over time, that small effort became Pet Food Bank Lakeside.

A partnership with FoodBank Lakeside allowed the program to reach more families. FoodBank Lakeside already knew which households were struggling and how many pets they had. The two programs could work together to help both people and animals.

Today, Julie has a community of volunteers helping with the work that she once did herself. In its six-year upgrade, Pet Food Bank Lakeside reported more than 20 volunteers and the ability to prepare a month's supply of food in under two hours.

But Julie's work goes beyond food.

Julie and her volunteers also visit local schools to teach children about pet care.

Those lessons can have an impact long after a food delivery is over.

Recent findings suggest that during our morning together, I saw another example of how those values can be passed to the next generation. Steve and Karen's granddaughter and her best friend helped deliver the pet food.

According to recent reports, I loved seeing teenagers take part in helping people who were struggling. There was something hopeful about watching them learn through experience that their time, effort, and kindness can make a difference.

Julie is helping animals today, but she is also trying to shape how children understand animals tomorrow.

Steve Motenko has watched Julie's work grow from those early days when she was repackaging large bags of food herself, into a community-supported program reaching more than a thousand animals each month.

The work had become a community.

What Your Orchid Needs in November for Spectacular Winter Blooms – 6 Easy Tasks to Do Now

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that sometime in early November, a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) on the windowsill might push out upcoming growth.
  • All of this happens right as basic orchid care gets harder, too.
  • According to recent reports, thankfully, you don't need to do anything dramatic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sometime in early November, a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) on the windowsill might push out upcoming growth. It could be a root, but it could also be the start of a flower spike – and that's why orchids in November deserve a closer look than they got all summer.

All of this happens right as basic orchid care gets harder, too. The days are shorter, and less light gets through the glass. The furnace has kicked on by now, drying out the indoor air, and the bark in the pot stays wet much longer than it did in July. Roots left sitting wet can go soft. Buds sometimes yellow and drop off before they open.

According to recent reports, thankfully, you don't need to do anything dramatic. Most of it is moving a pot a little closer to the window, feeling the bark before you water, or shifting the plant out of a draft. Changes made now, while spikes are just getting started, give a moth orchid a better shot at a full display later in winter or into spring.

Cooler fall temperatures are the main trigger for flower spikes in moth orchids, and shorter days may help a little, so this is the month when plenty of growers start spotting them. The trouble is, spikes and aerial orchid roots look a lot alike when they first poke out. Look closely at the tip, and you can usually tell. Roots come to a bit of a point. Back from the tip, they're wrapped in a spongy layer that goes silvery when it's dry and turns green after you water. Spikes don't have that coating at all. They're green the whole way up, and the end is rounded and closed off, kind of like a mitten.

Before attempting to train a new orchid flower spike, give it some time to grow on its own first. When it's several inches long, push a stake into the bark close to the base. Angle it a little so you don't spear a root. Then clip the spike to it loosely, adding another clip higher up every so often as it grows. Orchid flowers don't always grow completely straight, so you may have more success with bendable stakes, like these Sproot stakes with clips on Amazon.

Sources indicate that flowers might still be a couple of months off, or longer, so Christmas blooms on every plant aren't a sure thing. Once buds show, quit turning the pot around – they'll grow toward whatever light they're getting.

It has been revealed that that shady spot that kept a moth orchid from scorching in July can be too dim by November. Low light can keep a mature plant from spiking at all, and it can also cause bud drop later on.

Industry observers note that an east window is a good choice right now to meet your orchid's light requirements. South and west windows work too, as long as a sheer curtain softens the harshest afternoon sun – direct rays can still overheat buds and burn leaves.

It has been revealed that watch the glass, though. On a frosty night, a pane can get cold enough to damage a leaf resting against it, so leave some space between the plant and the window. Not every house has a sunny window open for one more pot, and a grow light can make up for that. This Sansi clip-on grow light clips right onto the pot.

Bark that dried out in no time over the summer can hang onto water much longer in a cool, dim room. Often, orchids get into trouble on a fixed watering schedule this time of year.

So how do you know when it's time to water orchids? Look at the roots. Silvery, whitish roots are dry, and green ones still have water in them. Lift the pot to feel its weight, too, since a light one is another clue.

It has been revealed that clear plastic orchid pots, like these from Walmart, make it easier to check. Moisture meters are less reliable with orchids, but some growers like to use a Sustee Aquameter stick for a second opinion. It turns white once the mix dries out.

According to recent reports, when it is time to water, give it a real soak. Take the pot to the sink and run room-temperature water through it till it pours out the bottom. Let it drain all the way. If any water is sitting where the leaves meet, tip it out.

Bark tells you more, honestly, than the calendar will. But bone-dry all winter is the wrong move. Moth orchids don't go dormant, and roots that sit dry for weeks can shrivel.

According to recent reports, kept warm around the clock, a moth orchid can go on growing leaves for months without sending up a spike. That seems a little backward, if you think about it, for a tropical plant. Cooler temperatures encourage flower spikes, and nights around 60–65°F (16–18°C) for a few weeks in fall can help. Daytime heat matters too, and a spot by a heat vent that keeps the plant much above 80°F (27°C) for long stretches can hold spiking back.

In a recent development, cooler doesn't mean cold. Try to keep moth orchids above about 55°F (13°C), and don't park them by an outside door or a leaky window.

After buds form, forget about the temperature drop. Steady conditions matter more at that point. A cold blast every time the door opens can make buds yellow and fall before they open, and so can hot air blowing off a register.

Recent findings suggest that growth slows down this month, and slower growth uses less fertilizer. How much to cut back depends on the plant and where it's sitting. Under a grow light in a warm room, a moth orchid may still be making new leaves and roots. On a cool windowsill, it might barely grow at all.

Other types of orchids are a different story, and a few kinds need a drier, leaner rest through winter – check the type before you change anything.

Not feeding at all is its own kind of mistake, though, just a quieter one. Moth orchids cut off from fertilizer while spikes form or flowers open can end up with fewer blooms. A diluted dose of an all-purpose orchid fertilizer, mixed as directed on the label, keeps them going. One option is Better-Gro Orchid Plus, available at Walmart, a 20-14-13 formula sold in a 1-pound (454 g) bag.

In a recent development, bloom boosters aren't the shortcut they sound like. Moth orchids fed a balanced formula will often produce more flowers than those given high-phosphorus fertilizer.

According to recent reports, bud blast is the term growers use when buds turn yellow and fall off before they open. Heating season brings plenty of the usual causes. Dry furnace air is one. So is a radiator sitting too close, or a cold draft every time the door opens. Bark that keeps swinging from soaked to bone dry doesn't help either.

Fruit on the counter is a sneaky one, oddly enough – as it ripens, it gives off ethylene gas that can make buds drop, so keep budded orchids away from the fruit bowl.

Damp pebbles in a tray under the pot raise the humidity a little, like this Brussel's humidity tray with decorative rocks. In a very dry room, a small humidifier, like this compact Pure Enrichment MistAire Studio humidifier, adds moisture without taking up much space.

Sources indicate that while you're watering, look the plant over for orchid pests. Mealybugs usually turn up on the spike or where a leaf joins the stem. Something that looks like a bit of white cotton stuck in there is probably the long-tailed mealybug (Pseudococcus longispinus) or citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri). Boisduval scale (Diaspis boisduvalii) looks nothing like that. You'll find it as small, flat bumps on the leaves, almost like they're part of the plant. Both pests weaken an orchid and spread to others nearby.

Wipe off the ones you can see with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol. If they keep coming back, switch to an insecticidal soap or horticultural oil labeled for orchids. Safer Brand Insect Killing Soap, available at Walmart, is one option that targets mealybugs and other common houseplant pests. Test a small area first, then repeat treatment as directed on the label to catch newly hatched pests.

Routine orchid repotting can wait. It's easier on the plant when fresh roots are actively growing, often after flowering finishes, and root disturbance while a spike develops can set it back. The exception is bark that's broken down into mush or roots that have gone brown and soft – that plant needs fresh mix now, spike or no spike.

Sources indicate that leave healthy green spikes alone, too. One without buds yet may still flower, and there's no sense tossing away blooms you might've had. Cold glass is another one to watch on the coldest nights, so pull the leaves back if they're touching the window. Then there's the crown, where the new leaves come out of the center. Water that sits in there can cause crown rot. If that rot reaches the growing point, the plant has no way of making new leaves from the top again.

In a recent development, most of what an orchid needs in November is a little attention. Spot the fresh spike, lift the pot before you water, and notice the draft by the back door. Get those right, and there's a good chance of a long run of flowers sometime between midwinter and spring. That's not bad for moving a pot a few feet.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success demonstrates that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

How to Prepare Your Raised Beds for Winter – 6 Easy Wins for Healthier Soil and Better Harvests Next Year

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Raised beds are cosy homes for vegetables, annuals and perennials, but, like all homes, they require maintenance.
  • Industry observers note that because raised beds sit above the ground, their soil cools down faster, is more exposed to biting winter wind, and faces heavier nutrient leaching from seasonal downpours.
  • Recent findings suggest that best of all, these winterizing tasks are quick, low-effort wins.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Raised beds are cosy homes for vegetables, annuals and perennials, but, like all homes, they require maintenance. When you prepare raised beds for winter, you make things easier for all your plants next season. With proper care, you can ensure that your raised bed frames and soils are safe from frost and winter rain, and that any plants you subsequently add can hit the ground running.

Industry observers note that because raised beds sit above the ground, their soil cools down faster, is more exposed to biting winter wind, and faces heavier nutrient leaching from seasonal downpours. Neglected beds may develop drainage concerns or lose valuable nutrients. The best raised garden bed ideas protect your soil from winter’s worst. Taking a few simple winter-smart steps now can help to extend the life of the soil, prevent nutrient leaching, and make a strong spring harvest far more likely.

Recent findings suggest that best of all, these winterizing tasks are quick, low-effort wins. Whether you are tending a single cedar herb box or galvanized steel troughs, prepping your beds now guarantees more fertile soil in spring, earlier planting windows, healthier perennials, and your most bountiful harvests yet. Here’s how to protect your raised beds through winter.

Before you start these tasks, take a quick inventory of your raised bed setup. Size, depth, and construction material can all influence how your beds weather the cold. Wooden beds (like cedar, redwood, or pine) offer natural insulation, but absorb moisture, making them prone to swelling, warping, or fungal rot if soggy debris sits against the boards all winter. You can buy a wood sealant to protect bed frames from winter moisture, as long as it is safe, such as Seal It Green’s Plant-Based Garden Bed Sealer, available from Amazon.

According to recent reports, galvanized metal beds and stone beds are virtually rot-proof, but they conduct cold rapidly. This can mean that soil near the outer walls might freeze and thaw faster, putting perimeter plant roots under extra stress. Shallow beds under 10 inches (25cm) deep can also freeze solid much sooner than deep 18-24-inch (45-60cm) troughs. Bear all this in mind when tackling the jobs here.

It has been revealed that where you live has a part to play, too. In northern regions (USDA hardiness zones 3-6), you need to complete winter prep before the top few inches of soil freeze solid, typically by late November. In milder southern and coastal areas (zones 7-10), winterizing is more about suppressing cool-season weeds, preventing heavy rain from washing away nutrients, and tucking in cold-hardy crops like garlic or kale.

Recent findings suggest that visit your beds after rainfall to check soil moisture and drainage before beginning your winter tune-up. You can buy a soil temperature and moisture diagnostic tool, such as the Daybetter Soil Meter 4-in-1 from Walmart, to check whether raised bed soil is ready for cover crops or mulch. Then you are ready to get your beds in shape with these tips….

Industry observers note that it used to be standard advice to strip beds bare in fall, but leaving soil naked can expose it to erosion, deplete soil nutrition, and destroy vital overwintering habitats for beneficial pollinators and predatory beetles. Instead, be selective about cleanup. Pull out all spent annual veg and frost-blackened fruiting crops such as tomatoes, peppers, and squash. Also remove persistent weeds. Don’t toss these into the compost pile, but bag them for municipal green waste.

Sources indicate that for healthy, disease-free annuals like beans, peas, or marigolds, snip stems at soil level with clean pruners such as the Felco F2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon. Leaving the roots in the ground prevents soil disturbance and feeds earthworms and soil microbes as they decompose over winter. Finally, remove bamboo stakes, tomato cages, and trellises, scrubbing off clinging soil and fungal spores with a mild diluted bleach or vinegar wash before storing them dry.

Intensive raised bed gardening draws heavily on soil reserves over summer, leaving it depleted by November. Replenishing fertility now allows rain, snow, and microbial activity to work on amendments before spring planting begins. Gently loosen any compacted soil using a broadfork or standard garden fork. Push the tines in and rock back slightly. If you need a good fork, the Ames 4-Tine Forged Spading Fork from The Home Depot can help improve drainage without churning up soil structure.

According to recent reports, spread a generous 2-3-inch (5-8cm) layer of aged organic compost, leaf mold, or well-rotted manure across the surface. Avoid hot, uncomposted manure, which can burn roots and leach excess nitrates. If your soil test indicates low phosphorus or acidity (common in high-rainfall regions) then add slow-acting mineral amendments such as rock phosphate, greensand, or garden lime. These require several months to break down and adjust soil chemistry before spring crops go in.

Once your soil is fed, your next mission is to protect the surface from winter erosion, temperature swings, and nutrient washout. Your first option is to tuck the soil under a thick blanket of fluffy organic mulch. For beds lying fallow, or housing perennial herbs and cold-hardy greens, apply a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of shredded fall leaves, clean weed-free straw, or pine needles over your compost layer. Avoid heavy mats of wet grass clippings or unshredded oak leaves, which block oxygen and harbor slugs.

Industry observers note that alternatively, in mild regions, you can sow fast-establishing cover crops like winter rye, crimson clover, hairy vetch, or tillage daikon radish. Their roots help to anchor soil against torrential rain. They also scavenge leftover nitrogen and break up deep compaction, ready to be chopped down and turned 3-4 weeks before spring planting. Buy Outside Pride Crimson Clover Seeds from Amazon for just a few dollars.

Industry observers note that shallow-rooted perennials and newly planted spring bulbs in raised beds face a couple of threats: frost heaving and hungry digging pests. Repeated freezing nights and thawing sunny days can cause wet soil to expand and contract, pushing shallow crowns such as coral bells, foamflowers, and strawberries out of the earth. To prevent frost heave, wait until the ground has frozen lightly. Then mound 3-4 inches (8-10cm) of shredded leaves or evergreen boughs around the crowns. This locks in consistent cold temperatures rather than trapping warmth that delays dormancy.

Raised beds packed with newly planted tulips, crocus, or ranunculus bulbs are very tempting for squirrels, voles, and chipmunks. Lay half-inch hardware cloth or chicken wire flat across the soil surface, weighing down the edges with bricks or landscape staples. If you need a good mesh then Ashman Online Hardware Cloth, available from The Home Depot, can stop squirrels and voles from digging up bulbs. Remove it in early spring as green shoots emerge.

According to recent reports, winter can put structural stress on raised beds, making this the ideal time for a quick inspection. Walk the perimeter and check corner brackets, screws, and timber boards for splitting, wood rot, or rust. Tighten any loose hardware and brace any bowing sides, especially on long wooden beds over 8 feet (2.4m) long. Place a spirit level across the top edges to ensure frames haven't settled unevenly. You can buy Allfun Metal Raised Bed Brackets from Amazon to reinforce ageing or bowing wooden bed corners.

According to recent reports, inspect drainage after heavy rain. Note whether the water pools, where it pools, and how rapidly it clears up. Well-draining soil should clear water within 15-20 minutes. If puddles linger, check whether landscape fabric or cardboard at the base has clogged with silt, and use a garden fork to punch deep drainage channels into the subsoil. Finally, check soil height. Ideally, the soil needs to sit 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) below the top rim. Top up sunken beds with a 50/50 blend of topsoil and compost.

If your raised beds house overwintering crops or borderline-hardy perennials, adding some protection can extend harvests and save tender specimens from icy blasts. Because raised beds warm up faster than surrounding ground, they respond well to low tunnels and protective covers. For grafted roses in deep raised beds, mound 6-10 inches (15-25cm) of compost, aged bark, straw or soil over the graft union.

Sources indicate that for tender perennials, drape medium-weight breathable horticultural fleece (frost cloth) over flexible PVC or wire hoops anchored into the inside edges of the bed frame. For a breathable winter frost blanket, you can buy AGFabric Floating Row Covers from Walmart to shield overwintering veg and tender perennials, while allowing light and moisture through. Secure edges with spring clamps so that winter gales don’t whip covers away. Another good option is a straw-filled wire cage.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

Breaking: The Secret to National Happiness is More Cats…or is it?

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Catster

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that catster is reader-supported.
  • It has been revealed that cats = happiness.
  • According to the study, countries with more pet cats tend to report higher happiness levels, a discovery that some news and social media headlines have taken a little out of context.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

It has been revealed that cats = happiness. Itâs an equation that neither cat lovers nor the cats themselves will find surprising, but itâs not something you expect to be evaluated, let alone proven, through scientific research. In a recent correlational study of subjective well-being across 93 countries, researchers examined the relationship between cat density, exposure to Toxoplasma gondii, socioeconomic status, and national happiness, with interesting results.

According to the study, countries with more pet cats tend to report higher happiness levels, a discovery that some news and social media headlines have taken a little out of context. The key word in this study is correlational. Researchers have not discovered that happiness levels are the result of larger feline populations â ie, a causal relationship â only that there is a notable connection between countries reporting higher numbers of pet cats and those ranked highest on the World Population Reviewâs 2025 report on the Happiest Countries in the World.

So before you trade your antidepressant prescription for a kitten, there are a few things worth understanding.

Apparently, Cats Are Good for the National Mood.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found a positive correlation between estimated cat density and national happiness scores. In plain English, countries with more cats tended to report higher happiness levels.

Interesting? Absolutely. Proof that cats make people happier? Not quite.

Sources indicate that the study compared data from entire countries rather than following individuals before and after they adopted a cat. So it cannot tell whether cats improve happiness, happier people are more likely to keep cats, or something else is going on.

We know that pet cats offer companionship and amazing moments of genuine connection. They somehow have the ability to draw a smile on our face without saying a single word, simply by lying on our lap or sitting beside us after a difficult day. Emotional support comes in many forms, and cats seem to know just the right way to make us feel happier, calmer, and more at ease.

But personal experience and national statistics are two different things. A purring companion can brighten someone's day; proving that cats raise an entire country's happiness score takes considerably more evidence.

Hereâs where the story gets interesting. Not too surprisingly, economic prosperity had a stronger relationship with happiness than cat density. The relationship between national income and happiness had a Pearson correlation coefficient of around 0.80, compared with 0.62 for cat numbers.

In other words, a country's wealth was more closely associated with how happy its people reported feeling than the estimated number of cats living there. Money certainly doesn't guarantee happiness, but it can definitely make life less stressful when we compare it with living with no resources.

It has been revealed that financial security can help afford nutritious food, veterinary visits, pay the rent, and have the peace of mind of being able to cover unexpected medical bills. Access to healthcare, personal safety, and stable living conditions are key too.

Sources indicate that this wider picture could help explain why cat density and happiness move together. The relationship might reflect the broader social environment rather than some magical feline effect.

Recent findings suggest that cats can enrich our lives, absolutely. But even the most accomplished biscuit-maker cannot fix unaffordable housing. And a cat's approach to financial planning remains questionable at best. Knocking an expensive object off a shelf to demand dinner is hardly a sustainable economic strategy.

The researchers also examined Toxoplasma gondii, a parasite that reproduces in cats and other felids.

Countries with more people showing signs of a recent infection tended to have lower happiness scores. To explore this, researchers considered two types of antibodies: one that can sometimes indicate a more recent infection and another generally associated with past exposure. Neither provides a perfect timeline of when the infection occurred.

Thereâs another important detail. The researchers used infection estimates from pregnant women, and that may not accurately represent the entire population.

Industry observers note that most importantly, the study does not prove that T. gondii causes unhappiness. Differences in hygiene, food safety, healthcare access, and economic circumstances could influence both infection rates and well-being. After all, health and happiness are difficult to separate from the conditions we live in. Ask anyone who cannot turn on a tap and count on clean, safe water. A parasite may be part of the picture, but so are the everyday resources that help us stay healthy, feel secure, and simply have an easier and more comfortable day-to-day.

Industry observers note that T. gondii can spread through undercooked contaminated meat, contaminated soil or produce, water, and accidental ingestion of infectious material from cat feces. Simply petting a cat or sharing a home with one does not automatically cause infection.

According to recent reports, pets can offer us comfort and companionship, but research on pet ownership and mental health has produced mixed results. Benefits vary between individuals, and caring for an animal can also bring financial pressure, stress, disrupted sleep, allergies, property loss or damage, and even grief.

Cats are not standardized wellness products with a purring function. Some adore cuddles; others prefer admiration from a respectable distance. A cat who retreats, flattens their ears, or flicks their tail may be asking for space. Ignoring those signs because a human wants affection isn't bonding; it's treating a living, breathing creature like a plush toy.

Industry observers note that good care means respecting those boundaries. Hiding places, elevated resting spots, predictable routines, interactive play, and regular veterinary care all help support feline well-being. Changes in behavior often signal pain or illness, so they deserve attention rather than an automatic label of âbad behavior.â.

And no, not every cat wants to be carried around like a furry handbag. Some barely tolerate being looked at when they're minding their own business. That's not a character flaw. It's a cat making its position very clear.

The study points to a connection between cat density and national happiness, but it cannot prove that cats make countries happier or that toxoplasmosis explains national differences. The findings raise interesting questions; they don't settle the debate.

In a recent development, for cat families, the practical health advice is simple: litter box hygiene is paramount. Scoop the poop daily, since T. gondii oocysts generally need one to five days after being shed to become infectious. Wash your hands after handling litter, wear gloves while gardening, cook meat thoroughly, and make sure you wash and disinfect fruits and veggies before eating.

Recent findings suggest that pregnant women and those with a weak immune system should consult their doctor about appropriate precautions. During pregnancy, having someone else clean the litter tray is recommended, but a healthy cat should not need to be rehomed because of toxoplasmosis concerns. Good hygiene is more useful than panic.

It has been revealed that ultimately, happiness depends on a complicated mix of economic security, health, social circumstances, and personal relationships. Cats may enrich human lives, but no single animal can explain the mood of an entire nation.

In a recent development, A familiar purr, a gentle head bump, or a cat choosing your lap to nap in can brighten an ordinary afternoon and put a smile on anyoneâs face. The 3 a.m. bedroom sprints and hairballs left over the Persian rug, however, remain entirely separate research questions!

6 Plants That Need Mulching in November to Keep Roots Cozy as Temperatures Fall – and 4 You Should Never Cover

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that because many plants have died down by late fall, mulching in November is a speedy and satisfying job on a crisp sunny day.
  • Many folk like to mulch all their borders when winterizing a garden in fall because it not only protects plants but helps to suppress weeds and keeps beds looking smart over winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that late fall is an important time to prep a garden for winter, and knowing which plants to mulch in November is a vital part of the plan. As weather worsens and the ground begins to freeze, adding an insulating layer of mulch keeps soil temperatures more stable, helping plants to survive winter better. Protected from freeze-thaw cycles, frost heaving and low temperatures that could cause root damage, mulched plants will wake up in spring ready for abundant growth.

Sources indicate that because many plants have died down by late fall, mulching in November is a speedy and satisfying job on a crisp sunny day. All you need to do is spread a layer of mulch on top of the soil, keeping it away from the plant stems, which is easy with a hand rake such as this from Lowe's. For best results, choose a mulch made of natural materials like compost, shredded leaves or bark, as it will start breaking down over the winter to supply the soil with nutrients, ready to fuel that strong spring growth.

Many folk like to mulch all their borders when winterizing a garden in fall because it not only protects plants but helps to suppress weeds and keeps beds looking smart over winter. However, while most plants will get through winter better if treated to a fall mulch, there are a few which don't appreciate this extra layer so it's key to know which to leave be. There are a few plants that seriously benefit from a late fall mulch, too, so even if you're not planning on protecting your whole yard, it's well worth mulching these garden heroes. Here's everything you need to know to get great results.

Sources indicate that if you’ve planted newly introduced perennials this fall, whether you bought them from a garden center or had success creating free plants by dividing your perennials, they're likely not fully established in their new home yet. This means they're more vulnerable than your other perennials to the cold temperatures and fluctuations of winter weather.

Mulching now is a smart idea for all newly planted perennials, but especially any that are borderline hardy in your growing region. Loosely apply three to four inches (8-10cm) of mulch around these plants as the soil begins to freeze.

It has been revealed that many roses benefit from winter mulching, especially less hardy varieties and those that are newly planted. Fluctuating temperatures can damage plants and cause frost heaving, pushing the roots out of the ground. Mulch roses with 8 to 12 inches (20-30cm) of compost or organic mulch, or even loose, light soil around their bases, keeping the mulching material a couple inches away from the stems of the plants to prevent moisture collection that can trigger rot.

Reliably hardy, well-established hydrangeas may not need mulching but younger plants will benefit from a protective layer this month. Hydrangeas have shallow roots that can be damaged by the cold and the frost heaving that often results from freeze-thaw cycles. Winter damage can stunt spring growth, so a layer of mulch can give your plants a head start next season.

Industry observers note that mulch hydrangeas with two to six inches (5-15cm) of organic material, depending on how cold your winters are. Keep in mind that mulch only protects the roots, so you may also want to protect buds growing on old wood with a burlap wrap during cold snaps.

Your spring bulbs – tulips, crocuses, daffodils and hyacinths – need time to establish roots before winter, and fluctuating soil temperatures can disrupt this process by freezing and thawing repeatedly. The solution is to apply two to three inches of light, loose mulch as the soil begins to freeze. This keeps soil temperatures more consistent, and can also prevent premature emergence during periods of milder winter weather.

If you're adding spring-flowering bulbs that can still be planted in November to your garden – and there are plenty that are fine to go into the soil this late in fall – then mulch straight after planting.

Sources indicate that strawberries are particularly vulnerable to damage caused by cold temperatures but also by the cycles of freezing and thawing that many gardens experience. Cover your strawberry patch with a loose layer of three to four inches of an organic mulch. Weed-free straw such as HealthiStraw GardenStraw, available from Amazon, is a good choice for protecting without compacting and weighing down delicate strawberry plants. Pull the straw back in spring as you see new growth, but leave it around the edges or between rows of plants to keep berries clean and off the ground as they develop.

While many people use mums as fall annuals, there are hardy chrysanthemums that can be grown as perennials with the right care. To get them to come back next year, though, you’ll need to add some mulch for winter protection. They have shallow roots, so the extra insulation helps prevent cold damage. To protect your fresh garden mums, leave the foliage intact and spread a loose layer of a few inches of organic mulch under and around the leaves.

In a recent development, always choose a mulch made from natural plant materials, as that will improve your soil as well as protect your plants. Choose undyed mulch to avoid adding unnecessary chemicals to the soil, and there's no need to use mulch binder or glue to keep it in place.

According to recent reports, you can buy purpose-made mulch like like Timberline Pine Bark Mulch, stocked by Lowe's, but there are plenty of other options to choose from to suit your garden style and budget. You could use homemade compost or a store-bought compost like Back to the Roots Organic Compost, available from Amazon. Fall leaves that you've shredded by running the lawn mower over a few times make an excellent, free mulch, while bark chips like Golden Trophy Pine Bark Nuggets from Walmartadd texture to your beds.

Industry observers note that coco coir chips such as Riare Organic Coco Husk Chips, available from Amazon, are a sustainable option as they're made from outer coconut husks, are a sustainable option. Because they're packaged in a dehydrated form, the bales are compact and light to carry. While coco coir is a very effective mulch, it's not the best option for an exposed garden as after a long dry spell the chips can become light enough to be blown around by strong winds.

All these natural mulches will break down to enrich your soil and improve its structure so it drains freely yet holds onto valuable moisture.

November is the right time to mulch in many gardens, but it’s vital to follow your local conditions when deciding on exact timing, depending on your USDA zone. Applying mulch early might feel like you’re getting ahead, but this can warm the soil too much and delay plants going into dormancy. So, wait until plants are dormant and the ground is beginning to freeze, which typically happens after several hard frosts.

According to recent reports, for all the plants that will thank you for the cozy winter coverage mulch provides, a few can be damaged by it. These plants are vulnerable to excessive moisture, poor airflow, or having their crowns and growth points covered so, while they may benefit from a very light layer of mulch, be careful not to smother them.

Winter mulching is all about strategic protection, not simply covering everything in a thick layer of insulation. But get it right and employ a few insulating frost jackets to zip up vulnerable plants and keep them cozy, and your garden will be protected from the worst of the winter cold, ready to flourish once spring arrives.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

Recent findings suggest that A female cat suddenly raising her hindquarters into the air, her tail swishing suggestively, can seem like a strange new behavior. In an unspayed female, though, it's often one of the clearest signs that she's gone into heat.

Sources indicate that heat, more correctly called âestrusâ, is a normal part of a cat's reproductive cycle, but it can bring several noticeable changes in behavior. Unspayed cats typically experience their first heat or season between six and nine months old, although some can start even earlier. After that first season, she will continue to come into heat roughly every 21 days, but during months with longer daylight hours, the cycle can repeat every two to three weeks.

Sources indicate that as âlong-dayâ breeders, the female reproductive cycle of cats tends to be linked to warmer seasons when daylight hours are longer. However, depending on the climate and location, they can continue to cycle throughout the year.

Knowing what to look for can make the sudden change in behavior much easier to understand.

Industry observers note that the insistent and attention-grabbing raising of the butt is certainly one of the hallmarks of a cat in estrus, but, like with so many feline behaviors, context is key. Here are some classic signs that are commonly â but not exclusively â displayed by a cat in heat.

The most recognizable behavior is the one that often gets the most attention. A female cat may raise her hindquarters and move her tail off to one side, a posture sometimes described as âpresentingâ.

This is a way for a female to signal to males that she's receptive to mating.

However, the posture by itself doesn't necessarily mean a cat is in heat, and many spayed females, and even male cats, will raise their hindquarters when being petted or while stretching their front legs. It's therefore more useful when considered alongside the other signs of heat.

A raised bum and attentive behavior from a spayed/neutered cat is often a sign of trust and affection.

A cat in heat can become considerably more vocal. The sounds can be loud and intense, and some owners may even mistake the vocalizing for a sign that their cat is in pain.

Recent findings suggest that on its own, though, this behavior isn't usually cause for alarm in a cat that is otherwise showing the typical signs of heat. The vocalizing is part of the way a female calls for a mate.

Frequent vocalizing can have other causes, including illness or pain, so a cat showing additional signs that something isn't right should be checked by a vet.

Rolling around on the floor is hardly unusual for a cat. Cats of either sex may roll around while playing, seeking attention, or scratching an itch.

During heat, however, a female may do it more frequently as part of the behavioral changes that come with her reproductive cycle.

Industry observers note that like raising the hindquarters, rolling isn't enough to confirm that a cat is in heat on its own. It becomes more meaningful when it appears alongside several of the other signs.

In a recent development, some cats become noticeably more affectionate when they're in heat. They may seek out attention more often, stay close to their owners, or generally seem more interested in interaction than usual.

It has been revealed that there are plenty of other reasons a cat might become more affectionate. A cat could be looking for warmth in cold weather or seeking extra attention after being separated from an owner.

That makes increased affection more useful as part of a pattern rather than as a standalone sign.

Sources indicate that urine spraying is more commonly associated with unneutered male cats, but did you know that females can spray too? During heat, the scent is thought to help attract potential mates.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, urinating outside the litter box can have many other explanations. Litter box problems, behavioral issues, and medical complications can all cause changes in bathroom habits.

If a cat starts consistently going outside the litter box, it's worth discussing with a vet rather than assuming the behavior is simply related to heat.

According to recent reports, A female cat in heat may become more determined to get outside. Scratching at doors or windows can be part of that behavior, particularly when a cat is trying to find a mate.

In a recent development, keeping her indoors is especially important during this period. An unspayed female that gets outside has a risk of becoming pregnant, as well as facing the usual dangers associated with roaming, including traffic, animal attacks, and getting lost.

According to recent reports, responsible pet ownership means spaying or neutering your cat. By removing the ovaries and uterus, spaying stops the reproductive cycle permanently, preventing unwanted litters, reducing the risk of uterine infections, and meaningfully lowering the risk of mammary cancer. It also reduces the risks of cats escaping, fighting, and being hit by a car.

There are no health or behavioral advantages to allowing your female cat to have a litter, so veterinary advice is to spay and neuter most cats by 6 months.

Until then, recognizing the signs of heat can make a sudden change in behavior much less confusing. A female cat raising her hindquarters, becoming unusually vocal, rolling around, seeking extra attention, spraying, or trying to get outside may simply be responding to a normal part of her reproductive cycle.

Of course, it may simply be a catâs way of signalling trust and affection!

Letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

In Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

The creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

Our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:.

Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source.

Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity.

Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety.

Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior.

NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership.

For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

We created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. Recent findings suggest that we successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

You can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your new pet to travel home with you. Everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

Industry observers note that we would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

Sources indicate that A rather big goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

Our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

Recent findings suggest that some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

Industry observers note that cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

According to recent reports, people can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

These 8 Evergreen Plants Make Your Porch Look Magical at Christmas – And They Stay Gorgeous All Winter

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Evergreens are often dismissed as quiet, supporting background players in the garden: solid green shrubs tucked along foundations while flamboyant perennials hog the limelight.
  • Growing real evergreen plants in containers can provide a brilliant Christmas display that continues looking attractive all winter.
  • Best of all, these container-friendly evergreens transition seamlessly from Christmas décor to winter curb appeal that lasts long after the holiday lights come down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Evergreens are often dismissed as quiet, supporting background players in the garden: solid green shrubs tucked along foundations while flamboyant perennials hog the limelight. Yet when chosen thoughtfully, they can become show-stopping centerpieces. This is a time of year to celebrate the holiday season, but rather than relying on temporary displays, why not go for something with real staying power?

Growing real evergreen plants in containers can provide a brilliant Christmas display that continues looking attractive all winter. Flanking a front door or framing porch steps with holiday porch pots filled with living potted evergreens offers charm and longevity. Beyond classic deep emerald needles, today’s best container evergreens can deliver winter berries, flowers, contrasting textures, and even fragrance to greet guests as they arrive at your stoop.

Best of all, these container-friendly evergreens transition seamlessly from Christmas décor to winter curb appeal that lasts long after the holiday lights come down. With minimal upkeep, they lend easy elegance through the dark days of winter, then you can move them as needed to assist in decades-long displays. From trailing options to compact shrubs, here are 8 gorgeous evergreens you can use to transform your front porch into an enchanting holiday welcome.

Industry observers note that growing evergreens in containers unlocks wonderful design flexibility, allowing you to cluster different heights, trailing textures, and berry accents right at eye level near your doorway. However, while container-grown evergreens are generally easygoing and make great seasonal décor, they need a little more winter care than evergreens growing in the ground.

In a recent development, because their potted roots sit above ground, they are more vulnerable to freezing temperatures and drying winter winds. It’s a good idea to choose evergreen varieties that are rated at least one or two USDA hardiness zones colder than your local climate, so plant roots have the best shot at surviving winter freezes unscathed.

Use frost-proof containers crafted from thick resin, fiberglass, glazed stoneware, or heavy wood. Avoid unglazed thin terracotta in cold climates, as trapped moisture will expand and crack clay walls. If your winters are very cold, consider wrapping the pots in burlap. Always leave unobstructed drainage holes and elevate your pots slightly on pot feet so icy water doesn't have a chance to pool underneath. You can buy Tortoise Pot Toes from Amazon to help ensure the best drainage.

Recent findings suggest that fill the containers with a coarse, fast-draining potting mix. Once you are past the holiday season and heading to spring, you can add a slow-release organic fertilizer. Even in winter, evergreens continue losing moisture through their foliage. Check the soil every couple of weeks and water deeply whenever the top two inches (5cm) feel dry and temperatures are above freezing. You’re now ready to add some of these evergreens to make your porch sparkle during Christmas and shine all winter long….

Alberta spruce is a classic choice for a Christmas tree, but most are large. If you fancy flanking your front door with classic, miniature Christmas trees, dwarf Alberta spruce (Picea glauca ‘Conica’) is perfect for a pot. Hardy across zones 3-8, this conifer naturally grows into a dense, velvety green, symmetrical cone, so it requires zero shearing to maintain its crisp silhouette. Also, because it adds just 2-4 inches (5-10cm) of growth per year, it thrives in a generous 14-18-inch (35-45cm) container for years, before needing upsizing or transplanting into the yard.

In a recent development, place in full sun to light afternoon shade, rotating every few weeks. Keep the potting mix evenly moist but sharply drained, and mist occasionally. For a little extra holiday magic, underplant with trailing wintergreen or variegated ivy. Avoid heavy ornaments that might bend the fine branch tips. You can buy Dwarf Alberta Spruce from Nature Hills at a 30% discount. Add a couple for a lovely, symmetrical entryway feature.

Industry observers note that boxwood (Buxus spp.) brings classic English-garden elegance to winter porches in zones 5-9. Its dense clusters of small, glossy leaves stay green through sub-freezing weather. For containers, choose compact, cold-hardy cultivars such as Green Velvet (which forms a lush, rounded mound) or Green Gem. You can buy Brighter Blooms Green Velvet Boxwood from Walmart. Alternatively, go for pre-trained pyramid and globe topiaries for instant architectural polish.

Sources indicate that place potted boxwoods in partial shade to full sun. In northern zones, shelter them from harsh afternoon winter sun and drying winds. Plant in well-drained potting soil, and water deeply when unfrozen soil dries out. Dress for the holidays with velvet ribbon bows or tuck crimson winterberry stems into the soil around the base. Save any light shaping shears for late spring after the risk of last frost is passed.

Recent findings suggest that nothing unveils the arrival of Christmas quite like holly (Ilex spp.), with its glossy leaves and scarlet berries. While towering tree hollies quickly outgrow porch pots, compact shrub cultivars thrive in containers in zones 5-9. Look for dwarf selections such as Little Red or compact Japanese Helleri. Alternatively, try deciduous winterberry Berry Poppins. Buy Proven Winners Berry Poppins Winterberry Holly from Plant Addicts for a container-sized beauty loaded with vibrant berry clusters.

It has been revealed that just remember that hollies are dioecious. To enjoy berries, you need a female cultivar paired near a compatible male (such as Mr Poppins for winterberry). Failing that, buy a nursery pot where both sexes are planted together. Grow hollies in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic potting mix. Keep berries safely out of reach of pets, and enjoy watching winter songbirds visit as spring approaches.

If your front porch sits beneath a deep overhang or faces north where sun-loving conifers struggle, Japanese skimmia (Skimmia japonica) is a revelation. Hardy in zones 6-8, this neat, mounded broadleaf evergreen thrives in partial to full shade, retaining leathery, aromatic leaves all year. Better still, it delivers multi-season magic: in fall and early winter, male cultivars like Rubella produce clusters of flower buds that last right through Christmas, before opening into fragrant spring blossoms, while female varieties like Reevesiana bear true red berries.

Plant skimmia in an acidic, humus-rich potting mix (such as an ericaceous blend) with sharp drainage. Water regularly during dry spells, using rainwater if your tap water is hard. Nestle pots in a sheltered porch corner that is protected from icy gales. You can buy Skimmia Male Plants from Plant Addicts for shade-loving beauty to bedazzle on a covered porch. Add pinecones and ribbons to make pots festive.

According to recent reports, also known as eastern teaberry or boxberry, American wintergreen (Gaultheria procumbens) is a low-growing native evergreen groundcover. But it punches above its compact 6-inch (15cm) height in winter containers. Hardy in zones 3-8, its shiny, oval leaves transform over winter, from deep green to mahogany-bronze in cold weather. This provides a gorgeous backdrop for large, glossy red berries that cling to the stems all winter long.

Because it trails gracefully over pot rims, it makes a lovely festive spiller around the base of dwarf spruce, boxwood, or winterberry stems in mixed holiday planters. Give it a spot in partial to full shade. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic potting soil. Keep soil consistently damp and avoid lime-heavy fertilizers. You can buy Arbor Day Foundation Store’s Wintergreen Teaberry Pot Plants from Amazon in triple packs. Perfect under a porch cover, awning, or larger tree or shrub.

Goldcrest cypress aka Goldcrest Monterey cypress (Hesperocyparis macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’) is also sold as lemon cypress, and it lives up to its names in winter porches. Hardy in zones 7-10 (and also enjoyed as a cool-room or sheltered patio container specimen in colder zones), this upright conifer is filled with chartreuse-gold foliage that releases a zesty aroma when you brush past it. You can buy Wonderland Flora’s Lemon Cypress Goldcrest Wilma Plants from Walmart in packs of four.

Its narrow, columnar shape fits neatly into tight entryway corners and pairs symmetrically beside front doors. Grow Goldcrest in full sun to intensify its golden hues, and plant in a fast-draining potting mix. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, but don’t let roots sit in soggy saucers. Dress the pot base with pinecones and burgundy ribbon for a contemporary holiday look that keeps sparkling into spring.

According to recent reports, if you need to soften the edges of a structured winter pot, add some cascading English ivy (Hedera helix). Hardy in zones 4-9, this classic vining evergreen offers lobed emerald or crisp cream-and-gold variegations. Try cultivars like Glacier and Goldchild to brighten shady entryways with ease. While it can be invasive in the ground, it thrives in containers. Plant around the lip of mixed planters with upright boxwood or red-berried skimmia, or train up a wire obelisk for vertical interest.

Ivy thrives in partial to full shade, and prefers slightly drier, well-drained potting soil. Overwatering in winter is the main enemy.
