Breaking: Every Japanese Maple Needs Some TLC Before Winter – 6 Easy Tasks to Protect Your Prized Tree

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As I write this, I cannot stop glancing at my Japanese maple, its entire canopy ablaze with crimson and orange foliage.
  • In a recent development, japanese maples (Acer palmatum) are counted among the most beautiful ornamental trees around, with their elegant branching structure, graceful canopy, and spectacular fall foliage.
  • So you should have more than a few items on your list for Japanese maple tree care before winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As I write this, I cannot stop glancing at my Japanese maple, its entire canopy ablaze with crimson and orange foliage. It's my little jewel of the garden, a sentiment shared by many of my friends with these small trees in their landscapes.

In a recent development, japanese maples (Acer palmatum) are counted among the most beautiful ornamental trees around, with their elegant branching structure, graceful canopy, and spectacular fall foliage. Since these trees are usually hardy down to USDA zone 4 or 5, they may shrug off winter cold. But that doesn’t make them immune to winter damage from the cold weather, harsh winds, and fluctuating soil moisture. Young trees and container trees are especially vulnerable.

So you should have more than a few items on your list for Japanese maple tree care before winter. If not, you’ve come to the right place. This guide explains the six simple but essential tasks to ensure your Japanese maple makes it through winter with flying colors. You can do them at the same time as your other garden winterizing tasks.

It has been revealed that don’t worry too much about watering your Japanese maple during winter. When the leaves fall and the tree enters dormancy, it needs very little water. Water trees only if there has been no precipitation for several weeks and the ground is bone dry.

Sources indicate that however, to help them through the winter, give them one final irrigation before the ground freezes. If the summer has been hot and/or dry, make this a deep watering. A soaker hose is ideal for delivering a slow, even soaking across the tree's root zone without wasting water. The Gilmour Round Soaker Hose from Amazon is a good option, as it distributes water evenly along its length.

According to recent reports, tuck a cozy blanket of mulch around your precious tree in November. Use something organic – wood chips or bark work well. Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot is a good option, made from natural, shredded wood. Layer up to 4 inches (10 cm) of mulch over the root zone. This protects the roots, holds heat in the soil, and prevents frost heaving.

Don’t make the mistake of piling the mulch up against the trunk in a “volcano” arrangement. The mulch should never touch the trunk since that can cause wood rot.

Sources indicate that is your Japanese maple a young tree you planted within the last three years? You’ll want to give the juvenile tree extra protection. This will also be true if you live in a region with an exceptionally cold winter.

According to recent reports, in these circumstances, help your tree survive with insulation. Wrap vulnerable trunks or branches with burlap, such as this Riare Natural Burlap Plant Protection Wrap from Amazon, to shield them against harsh, drying winter winds. Leave the burlap loose enough to allow the tree to breathe.

If your tree has broken or diseased branches, the best time to take those off is now, whenever you notice. And you should check regularly to spot problems early. But aside from this type of damage, do not give your Japanese maple a haircut in November or at any other point during dormancy. Pruning at this time can leave cuts vulnerable to disease and frost damage.

In a recent development, would you have an energy drink just before bedtime? Of course not. And for all the same reasons, do not fertilize your Japanese maple in November. Fertilizer, especially nitrogen fertilizer, induces newly introduced growth just as the tree should be entering winter dormancy. This new growth is tender and will easily freeze in the first flush of winter weather, leading to dieback or split bark.

In spring, if your tree needs feeding, use a gentle, slow-release fertilizer, such as Espoma Organic Tree-tone (6-3-2) from Amazon. Apply sparingly, following the package instructions, as Japanese maples generally don't need much fertilizer.

It won’t surprise you to hear that container maple trees require more protection than a Japanese maple with its roots deep in the garden soil. Their roots are much closer to the cold air on all sides, and therefore can freeze or dry out faster.

In a recent development, you’ll want to take steps to protect a potted Japanese maple. A good first step is to insulate the containers with bubble wrap or burlap. Wrap the pots well and cluster the containers together near the house to attract radiant heat. It also helps to use pot feet, like Bosmere's Pot Toes, or even wood blocks to raise the containers off the cold ground and support good drainage.

In the most severe winters, you can move your container trees into a shelter, like an unheated garage or a sheltered porch.

Sources indicate that does your tree still have leaves as Thanksgiving arrives? This is normal, not a cause for alarm.

Trees have an abscission layer at the base of their leaf stems that releases the leaves to fall in the cold. But Japanese maples build this layer more slowly than other deciduous trees like red or sugar maples. And if you’ve had a mild autumn, this can delay leaf drop even further, even into December.

According to recent reports, this means additional watering work for you. While your maple still has leaves, you’ll need to keep watering whenever the soil is dry. At the same time, rake up leaves that do fall and remove them. You don’t want soggy or decaying piles of maple leaves since this can encourage the spread of fungal spores.

She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler at the moment splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

70+ Dogs Rescued From South Korean Meat Farm as 2027 Ban Approaches

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dogster

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that dogster is reader-supported.
  • Nearly 30 dogs have arrived in Newly introduced York after being rescued from a dog-meat farm in South Korea.
  • A plane ride to Upcoming York probably wasn't on these dogs' bingo cards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

Nearly 30 dogs have arrived in Newly introduced York after being rescued from a dog-meat farm in South Korea. Their journey toward adoption is beginning, but with the country's ban still months away from taking full effect, the work is far from over.

A plane ride to Upcoming York probably wasn't on these dogs' bingo cards. Neither, for that matter, was a soft bed, a full bowl of food, or the chance to be someone's beloved family member. After spending their lives confined to cages, even the simplest things may seem exciting and new.

It has been revealed that on October 1, nearly 30 dogs were rescued from a dog-meat farm in Gangjin, South Korea, that once bred and slaughtered as many as 1,000 dogs each year. This was part of a larger rescue operation by Humane World for Animals that saved more than 70 dogs from the property.

For the organization, the operation marks its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea ahead of the country's ban, which takes full effect on February 7, 2027. Humane World for Animals has rescued nearly 3,000 dogs from farms since 2015, making this a significant milestone.

Recent findings suggest that and yes, it's a reason to celebrate. But before we get too comfortable patting ourselves on the back, there's a much bigger picture to consider. Getting these dogs out was a huge victory, but there are still thousands at risk.

Sources indicate that when the rescue team arrived at the farm in Gangjin, in South Korea's South Jeolla Province, they were met with disturbing scenes. Rows of rusting cages, abandoned collars scattered on the ground, and skeletal remains served as a gruesome reminder of the dogs that hadn't been so lucky.

Industry observers note that it's a hard reality to come to terms with, especially if your own dog is at the moment hogging the sofa, demanding snacks, or staring at you as though you've ruined their life by being five minutes late with dinner. The minor dramas faced by our beloved pets are a world away from what these poor dogs endured.

According to recent reports, humane World for Animals has reported finding mixed breeds and dogs of different sizes during its rescue work. The survivors included Jindos, a breed native to South Korea, a husky mix, and smaller dogs, including a spitz mix. In other words, any dog could end up on the menu.

Industry observers note that in this most recent rescue, a concerned citizen alerted a local animal protection group, which contacted Humane World for Animals and the authorities. Officials found that the farm had broken South Korea's Animal Protection Act. The farmer, a man in his 80s, agreed to hand over the dogs and promised not to take part in the dog-meat trade again.

More than 70 dogs were rescued. Nearly 30 travelled to New York, another 12 went to a rehabilitation center in Montreal, and some mothers and their puppies remained in South Korea because they were too young to fly safely.

Recent findings suggest that rescuing dogs from situations like this isn't as simple as just opening a cage and booking the next available flight. International transport requires veterinary checks, vaccinations, documentation, and careful consideration about which animals are fit to travel. The priority is getting them out safely, not rushing them onto a plane for the sake of a happy headline.

In a recent development, south Korea passed its Special Act on the Termination of Breeding, Slaughter, and Distribution of Dogs for Consumption in January 2024. Its key prohibitions will finally take full effect on February 7, 2027, making it illegal to breed, slaughter, or sell dogs or dog meat for human consumption. But the transition is already underway.

In May 2026, South Korea's Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs reported that about 82% of the country's 1,537 registered dog-meat farms had closed. Over a thousand farms closed is something worth celebrating, but it means 272 farms are still operating.

Another consideration is that closing a farm doesn't automatically save the dogs living there. A business can shut down, the gates can close, and the paperwork can be signed, but where do all those dogs go?

According to Humane World for Animals, government figures indicate that of approximately 393,857 dogs counted on farms that had been closed, only 1,121 were adopted or transferred to public shelters. That's about 0.3%.

It has been revealed that itâs understood that most of these dogs were sent for slaughter or moved to other farms. Just because you like gardening doesn’t mean that you enjoy every landscape task. Some of us gardeners love planting flowers but don’t enjoy raking leaves. Others like tucking mulch around their shrubs but won’t pull weeds. But digging up the garden dirt and turning it over is not high on anyone’s list of favorite tasks.

In a recent development, so just say no to digging in the fall and say yes to lasagna gardening. It’s a clever, no-dig technique that works best in fall. Leave the shovel in the garage and instead, stack layers of cardboard, fallen leaves, and other organic materials over the garden soil, letting them break down naturally over winter. The result is fertile planting beds for spring.

Sources indicate that ready to get “cooking”? Here, I will walk you through the four-layer lasagna garden recipe.

Of course you love your garden, but wouldn’t it be nice if the garden could do most of the work of preparing the beds for spring planting? Lasagna gardening, aka no-dig or no-till gardening, allows your garden to do most of the work of decomposition and replenishment. The technique is really cold composting in place.

Industry observers note that this low-effort process works like home composting: alternate layers of green and brown materials, then let them break down into the soil. Cut grass and kitchen scraps are green materials; cardboard and dried leaves are brown materials. Your “lasagna” is a compost heap waiting to happen.

Recent findings suggest that you can also think of lasagna gardening as mimicking the forest floor. It works the same way soil is built up in a woodland. First, leaves pile up and decompose on the forest floor. Along come microbes and worms that transform that debris into rich soil. Lasagna gardening follows the same pattern, making your garden bed into a soil ecosystem.

According to recent reports, when you make a lasagna for dinner, you just layer up the pasta, the ragù, the sauce, and grated cheese, then pop it in the oven. Without any additional work on your part, a luscious dinner will be ready when it is time to eat.

According to recent reports, A winter lasagna garden uses the same system. You stack up four layers, then leave it to decompose. Without any additional work on your part, your garden will have rich, fertile soil for spring. Here are the four key layers.

Industry observers note that think of cardboard as the weed barrier. First, weed-whack or mow the area to cut down any weeds or grass. A cordless string trimmer, like this Worx model, makes things easier.

It has been revealed that then, lay sheets of flattened cardboard right over the soil in your garden, using overlapping layers to cover the entire area. Heavy, corrugated cardboard works best to keep grass and weeds out while still welcoming earthworms. After that is done, douse all of the cardboard with lukewarm water.

Sources indicate that this is the carbon layer, supporting soil microbes and providing structural aeration. I like using dry autumn leaves (what else are you going to do with them?), but a thick layer of any type of brown material will work, giving your garden soil a carbon-rich environment. Alternatives include straw, peat moss, sawdust, wood chips, or shredded newspaper.

If you don't have enough waste materials to hand, a bag of garden straw mulch, like this HealthiStraw GardenStraw from Walmart, is an easy way to bulk up this layer.

According to recent reports, here’s the “compost” element of the lasagna. Your green materials will be in charge of making the garden soil a nitrogen-rich environment that heats up and fuels the decay process. Together with the brown material, they make the garden one giant compost pile. You can use kitchen waste, but also toss in some grass clippings, coffee grounds, or even manure.

If you can't source enough green material for free, then pick up a bag of composted cow manure, such as Black Kow, available at Home Depot.

You aren’t limited to one layer of brown material and one layer of green. Keep right on stacking alternating layers, using about twice as much brown as green. Two, three, or even four alternating layers of organic material can speed things up for your garden bed.

Recent findings suggest that flattened cardboard lays the foundation for the lasagna; compost or topsoil serves as a top cap. For a ready-made option, try Back to the Roots Organic Compost from Home Depot. This is especially vital if you are planning on planting immediately. This rich layer is at the top of the pile so that your seeds will have what it takes to establish strong roots in short order.

A lasagna garden is an attractive option if low-maintenance is a priority. Once you create your lasagna, wonderful things begin to happen and keep on happening all winter. The green and brown layered materials function as a compost pile, and the constant interplay between them heats up, then breaks down the entire pile, enriching the soil.

The bottom layer of cardboard in the garden lasagna blocks weeds from invading the new, appealing soil. What had been a used-up garden transforms into a sanctuary for your plants, with loose, fertile soil. This makes the next growing season easy and exciting.

Recent findings suggest that if you “build” a lasagna garden in the late autumn or early winter, the magic starts right away. The four layers do their job: the cardboard prevents weed growth, the brown and green layers do their compost dance and decompose into the soil, and the top layer is ready to welcome seeds.

This lasagna garden should be fully decomposed and ready to plant by the following April or May. Autumn rain and winter moisture keep the layers moist. The organic layers require at least several months to break down.

Industry observers note that if you put in a lasagna garden in spring or summer, you do so with the thought of immediate planting. Just dig small pockets into the top layer of the bed.

Industry observers note that long before the United States military established an official war dog program, one small stray taught the Army what a dog could do in combat. His name was Stubby, and by the time the First World War ended, he had become the most decorated dog in American military history.

According to recent reports, stubbyâs story began in the summer of 1917 at Yale Field in Newly introduced Haven, Connecticut, where the 102nd Infantry Regiment of the 26th âYankeeâ Division was training before deployment to France. A short-tailed, brindle-colored dog of uncertain breeding, likely part Boston terrier and part American bull terrier, wandered into camp and was adopted by Private J. Robert Conroy. Soldiers were not permitted to keep pets, but Stubby won over the men, and eventually the officers, by learning to mimic military customs. He reportedly marched in step with the troops and raised a paw to his brow in a passable salute.

Industry observers note that when the 102nd Infantry shipped out for France, the transport ships barred dogs. Conroy smuggled Stubby aboard the SS Minnesota hidden beneath his overcoat. Conroyâs commanding officer discovered Stubby during the crossing, but his salute reportedly charmed the officer into letting him stay.

According to recent reports, once in France, Stubbyâs role shifted from morale booster to something closer to that of a working soldier. He entered combat on February 5, 1918, at Chemin des Dames, enduring shelling for over a month, and went on to serve through 17 battles over 18 months on the Western Front.

According to recent reports, after surviving a mustard gas attack, Stubby developed a heightened sensitivity to the smell of gas. Historians and contemporary newspaper accounts credit him with warning his regiment of subsequent gas attacks before the men could detect it themselves. This allowed soldiers time to don their masks. He was also credited with locating wounded soldiers in no manâs land and comforting them until stretcher bearers arrived.

It has been revealed that stubbyâs most famous exploit occurred when he discovered a German soldier mapping the layout of Allied trenches. According to accounts preserved by military historians, Stubby seized the man until American soldiers arrived to take him prisoner. For this act, Stubby was informally promoted to the rank of sergeant, making him, according to most accounts, the first dog to receive a rank in the United States Armed Forces. This was, of course, an honorary and unofficial designation rather than a formal commission, since the military does not commission dogs.

It has been revealed that during the April 1918 German offensive on the town of Seicheprey, France, Stubby was wounded in the chest and leg by grenade shrapnel while accompanying the 102nd Infantry in combat. After recovering, he returned to visiting wounded soldiers in the hospital, walking the wards to lift the spirits of recovering men.

Harding, and Calvin Coolidge. General John J. Pershing personally honored him at a 1921 ceremony for the 102nd Infantry Regiment, presenting him with a gold medal from the Humane Education Society, an award that, while not an official military commendation, cemented his reputation as the greatest war dog of his era.

In a recent development, conroy went on to attend Georgetown University Law Center, and Stubby went with him, becoming the unofficial mascot of the Georgetown Hoyas football team. At halftime, he would nudge a football around the field to the delight of the crowd.

In a recent development, stubby died in 1929, reportedly in Conroyâs arms. His remains were preserved and are held today by the Smithsonianâs National Museum of American History, where he wears the medals and blanket he wore during his years of service. In 2018, an animated film called Sgt. Stubby: An American Hero introduced his story to a latest generation. That same year, the descendants of Conroy dedicated a life-sized bronze statue of him at the Connecticut Trees of Honor Memorial in Middletown, Connecticut.

Sources indicate that stubby served nearly a quarter century before the United States Army established a formal War Dog Program in 1942. He had no training pipeline, no breeding program, and no structure to recognize what he did. He was, in the truest sense, an amateur who became indispensable through instinct, loyalty, and repeated exposure to danger alongside the men who fed and sheltered him. Later advocates of formal military working dog programs often cite his legacy as early proof of concept: a dogâs senses, courage, and bond with a handler could save human lives on a modern battlefield.

According to recent reports, every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

It has been revealed that keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Sources indicate that follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

Recent findings suggest that if Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

I have a question about my dog, Jethro. Sometimes when he alerts, the hackles between his shoulders rise. Other times they are prominent along his lower back. What does each appearance indicate about how he is responding?â.

In a recent development, that is a great observation! When a dogâs hackles rise, it is an involuntary response controlled by the autonomic nervous system called piloerection, and it tells us that his arousal level has increased. However, the location of the raised hair does not reliably tell us which emotion a dog is experiencing.

Recent findings suggest that when the hackles rise between his shoulders, it can accompany alertness, excitement, uncertainty, or concern. When they appear along his lower back, the same range of emotional responses is possible. Neither pattern automatically indicates aggression, fear, or a particular level of threat. Think of hackles as a little emotional alarm bell; they tell us Jethro is experiencing heightened arousal, but not exactly why.

Industry observers note that different dogs will respond to different stimuli in different ways, so thereâs no âone size fits allâ explanation for why different areas are triggered. I would pay close attention to what is happening around him when this occurs. Is he alerting to a stranger approaching the house, another dog walking past, an unfamiliar noise, or something unexpected in the environment? You might want to start keeping a record of what is going on before and after Jethroâs hackles are raised, and whether itâs his shoulders or lower back that is involved.

Industry observers note that combine that context with his facial expression, ear position, tail carriage, posture, muscle tension, and ability to disengage. Looking at the whole picture helps us understand whether Jethro is curious, excited, uncertain, or uncomfortable, and, most importantly, how we can best support him. These details, together with what triggered the alert, give us a much clearer picture of how Jethro is feeling.

In a recent development, eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling are one of those celebrity couples that keep their heads down and their private lives just that; private. So sue us, then, that we get excited when they offer us a sneak-peek into their world... especially when it comes with a Christmassy twist!

Recent findings suggest that now, we usually think of a Christmas tree as being larger than life, and twice, especially when it's in the home of a celebrity. Honestly, though, most stars seem to be taking a laidback approach to their festive decor of late, whether it's the Beckhams' bow-filled Christmas tree, Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, or even Michelle Obama's twig tree.

Eva and Ryan have opted for a similarly unfussy approach; the couple's kitchen island is full of miniature Christmas trees. Check it out:.

A post shared by Eva Mendes (@evamendes).

And just like that, they've proven you don’t need a large traditional evergreen tree to make your house look stylish during the holidays. In fact, if you decide to follow in Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling's footsteps, you might not need to buy much at all.

All you have to do is take a simple stroll around your garden with a pair of pruners and a small pot to get the same look; fortunately, some experts told me exactly how to do it.

“The best mini Christmas trees start with a walk around your own garden,” indicates Nick Alan, founder of Palma Botanical Co., who has been growing plants for 25 years.

In a recent development, his picks? “Conifer tips like cedar, cypress, juniper and fir hold their needles longest. Boxwood and rosemary fill gaps and add scent.”.

For clean cuts, Nick Alan recommends these Fiskars SoftGrip bypass pruners.

Sources indicate that use gentle hands with the shrub, though. “Harvest on a cool morning with clean pruners, cutting just above a side shoot so the plant regrows, and take no more than a third of any shrub,” says Alan.

Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, has a simple pot method for getting the Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling look this Christmas.

“Fill a 4-inch pot with damp sand (this will help hold your stems upright and will allow you to leave the tree in its pot as it dries). Remove the needles from the bottom 2 inches of each stem (you don’t want any foliage to rot in the sand!).”.

Sources indicate that once this is done, she says you should “arrange the stems from tallest in the middle to shortest as you work your way out (creating a cone shape).” Remember, though, that cut foliage won’t last forever. “Mist every few days and keep it away from the stove, dishwasher vent, and sunny windows. Expect two to three weeks, swapping tired sprigs,” says Alan.

A living tree means you don’t have the extra work of worrying about sprigs. “For a kitchen island display like Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling's, I like a living miniature tree best, because it does two jobs at once: it looks festive, and it stays useful after Christmas,” says Morgan Brooks, founder and editor of Plant Style Home.

Brooks indicates rosemary is the practical pick for a kitchen: “Rosemary is the most practical in a kitchen because you can pick sprigs for cooking, and it smells wonderful near the stove.”.

For care, Brooks says: “I keep young trees in cool spots away from radiators and water the compost so it stays lightly damp but never wet.” Alan adds: “Give it your brightest window, water when the top inch is dry, and plant it out afterward in zone 8 and warmer.”.

Shop Live Rosemary Christmas Trees:.

Your kitchen island may be a great spot for trees, but don’t forget it’s also a workspace for cooking. Keep your trees all to one side and never let them near heat sources, especially the dry foliage.

Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, states that “a little greenery with one beautiful ribbon often looks more considered than a crowded arrangement.”.

Sources indicate that for the layout, Melam states: “I love displaying mini trees in odd-numbered clusters of varying heights. Negative space is key! I’d keep the tallest stem 10-12 inches so as not to compete with faucets, etc.”.

A tray helps too: “Displaying them on a tray or wooden slab can help tie them together & unify the display (as opposed to them looking like random pots on a counter).” On a budget, Alan says: “Pine cones, dried orange slices and ribbon dress them cheaply.”.

Alan has one note of advice for people with pets or small children: “Skip holly, yew and mistletoe around pets and kids, since all are toxic.”.

While Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling have both played a variety of characters throughout their film careers, we really do think that “people with a stunning Christmas kitchen island” is one we really fancy having a go at, too.

Hyperactivity is common, and the good news is that knowing what causes it makes it much easier to help a puppy calm down. The reasons range from ordinary puppy exuberance to, on rare occasions, a health problem.

In a recent development, puppies burn energy by exploring and playing, but they can run out of things to do. A mix of toys, activities, and walks helps manage their energy. Without it, boredom and frustration can lead to destructive behavior or aggression, or to zooming around the house. A puppy with no good outlet, such as a sturdy chew toy, will release that pent-up energy by barking, running around, or jumping on people.

The opposite problem is just as real. Just like toddlers who throw tantrums when theyâre overtired, puppies that have too much going on can become hyperactive because they donât understand that they need a nap, and the discomfort frustrates them. Finding the balance gets easier as an owner learns a puppyâs energy levels. Plenty of activities and training sessions help, as do regular quiet times for cooling off and a quick nap to recharge.

Sources indicate that puppies learn promptly, and that includes behaviors that owners donât mean to encourage. If a puppy gets attention every time it becomes overexcited during play, even when the owner is trying to say stop, the puppy sees it as a reward, and the next time it feels neglected, hyper behavior may seem like a good way to get noticed. The fix is to interact when the puppy is gentle or relaxed, and to become less interesting when it gets overexcited, by dropping the tug toy and stepping away.

According to recent reports, all puppies have energy, but the amount varies by breed, and a breedâs original purpose matters as much as its size. Border Collies, bred to herd sheep all day, require lots of physical and mental stimulation to keep up with their boundless energy. A more sedate breed, like the French Bulldog or King Charles Spaniel, tends to have far less energy to burn. A Border Collie puppy has less stamina than an adult, but it still has plenty of energy to manage.

Food affects everything from digestion to brain development, and it can influence sleep cycles, energy levels, and skin health. The wrong diet may contain too much of certain ingredients, often protein, which can lead to hyperactivity. Researching a puppyâs nutritional needs and checking the ingredients with a vet is worthwhile.

Obedience training teaches a dog how to manage its behavior, and socialization helps it get used to people, other pets, and latest situations. Without them, a puppy doesnât know how to react, and a quick play session can end with an overexcited puppy that canât calm down. A tiny puppy climbing on people or nipping fingers may seem cute, but puppies donât always stay small, and an adult dog that bites or jumps can be dangerous, especially around a child or a stranger.

Most of the time, hyperactivity is easily corrected and comes down to diet, breed, or limited exercise. Health problems are a rare cause. If a puppy is still hyper after changes to diet, activity, and training, a vet check to rule out any health issues is always a good idea. The earlier a problem is diagnosed, the easier it is to treat.

Puppies are still learning what their bodies are telling them. One of the most common signs is becoming hyper or restless when they need to go. An older puppy getting used to house training may be asking to go out, while a younger one may not understand the signal and burst into a case of the zoomies until it figures it out.

Most hyperactivity simply comes from being a puppy. Younger dogs are more excitable, and they need lots of energy to explore the world without yet knowing how to manage it. Puppies steadily grow out of it. They may still get the zoomies later on, but they settle and learn better control. Rewarding calm behavior, working on obedience, and giving a working breed a job to do all help.

Researching a breed before bringing a puppy home matters, since a high-energy herding breed can be too much for some households. Time matters too, because a long workday followed by evening chores may leave little room for the exercise a puppy needs.

According to recent reports, activity is the best way to manage energy, and it shouldnât be only physical. Puzzles and other mental activities keep a brain busy as well. Training helps too, because some hyper behavior is really bad manners learned along the way, such as jumping up or racing around when the leash comes out.

Most puppies grow out of their boundless energy as they reach adulthood and learn self-control, which can take between one and two years depending on breed. Some breeds are naturally quieter and happier to laze around, while more active breeds never lose their energy. A routine tailored to a dogâs needs is essential, along with choosing a puppy that suits the family.

It has been revealed that if Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

According to recent reports, chips was a mix of German Shepherd, Collie, and Husky, born around 1940 and raised as a family pet by Edward Wren and his family in Pleasantville, Newly introduced York. In 1942, the Wrens donated Chips to the newly formed Dogs for Defense program, part of the Armyâs larger War Dog Program, formally authorized on March 13, 1942. Chips trained at the War Dog Training Center in Front Royal, Virginia, and was partnered with Private John P. Rowell. The two served in the 3rd Military Police Platoon, 30th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, under General George S. Patton.

Chips and Rowell landed in North Africa during Operation Torch in November 1942 and served through campaigns in Sicily, Italy, southern France, and the Rhineland and central European theaters. He was also present as a sentry dog at the 1943 Casablanca Conference, guarding the meeting between Winteon Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Chips earned his fame during the Allied invasion of Sicily, Operation Husky, on the morning of July 10, 1943. As Rowell and Chips came ashore, a hidden machine gun nest opened fire and pinned down their platoon. Chips tore free of his handler and charged the position alone, seizing the gunner by the throat and forcing the crew to surrender. As a result, four Italian soldiers surrendered. That same night, Chips alerted the platoon to ten additional enemy soldiers attempting to slip through the lines under cover of darkness, leading to their capture as well.

Chips did not escape the encounter unscathed. He suffered burns around his mouth and eye and a wound to his scalp. His actions, however, swiftly became national news. Captain Edward G. Parr, the company commander, recommended Chips for the Distinguished Service Cross, citing his âcourageous action in single-handedly eliminating a dangerous machine gun nest and causing surrender of its crewâ. On November 19, 1943, Major General Lucian K. Truscott Jr. awarded Chips the Silver Star, and accounts differ slightly on whether the Distinguished Service Cross was also formally conferred or only recommended. What is well documented is that Chips also received a Purple Heart for his wounds.

In a recent development, in 1945, Chips met General Dwight (Ike) D. Eisenhower, who bent down to pet the famous dog. Chips, true to his sentry training, nipped the generalâs hand. The incident became one of the more good-humored footnotes in his legend.

In a recent development, washington reacted less good-humoredly to the idea of a dog receiving human military honors. After public objection to the precedent of awarding animals medals intended for soldiers, the War Department revoked Chipsâs Silver Star, Distinguished Service Cross, and Purple Heart in early 1944. His platoon nonetheless unofficially awarded him a Theater Ribbon with Arrowhead, an honor reserved for assault landings, along with eight battle stars, one for each campaign in which he served. Chips was honorably discharged on December 10, 1945, and returned to the Wren family in Pleasantville. He died a few months after returning home, from complications related to his wartime wounds.

Sources indicate that in January 2018, more than seven decades after his service, the United Kingdomâs PDSA posthumously awarded Chips its Dickin Medal, the animal equivalent of the Victoria Cross, in a ceremony at the Churchill War Rooms in London on the 75th anniversary of the Casablanca Conference. John Wren, then 76, traveled from the United States to accept the medal on Chipsâs behalf. PDSA Director General Jan McLoughlin remarked that the honor finally allowed Chips to âtake his place in the history books as one of the most heroic dogs to serve with the US Armyâ.

Chips is estimated to have been one of more than 10,000 dogs who served in the American military during World War II. His story, and the controversy his medals caused, shaped military policy for decades: no American war dog would again receive an official human combat decoration, a policy that held until working dogs began receiving other forms of formal recognition much later in the twentieth century.

According to recent reports, every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

According to recent reports, support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

It has been revealed that learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

It has been revealed that keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

It has been revealed that these dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

Among the dogs of the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record. Scout Dog York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

Don't Buy a Poinsettia Until You've Checked This Tiny Detail – It Reveals How Long It Will Last

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it happens every December.
  • Some of that can be blamed on poinsettia care after you get home, like a cold windowsill or a pot left sitting in water.
  • It has been revealed that there's an easy way to tell a fresh one from a tired one, and hardly anybody looks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it happens every December. You bring home a full, bright red poinsettia, set it on the table, and a week or two later the colorful bracts start to curl and fall. By Christmas morning, the plant looks tired and half bare.

Some of that can be blamed on poinsettia care after you get home, like a cold windowsill or a pot left sitting in water. Much of it starts at the store, though. The plant was already on its way out before it ever went in the cart.

It has been revealed that there's an easy way to tell a fresh one from a tired one, and hardly anybody looks. Forget the red for a second. Down in the center of each cluster of colored leaves are some tiny yellow-green buds, and those say a lot more about how long the color will hold up. It's kind of a strange thing to judge a plant by, but trust the process.

Those colorful "petals" on a poinsettia aren't petals at all. They're bracts, and they color up in fall as the nights get longer. Right in the middle sit the real flowers, small knobby clusters called cyathia. Each one is a little cup holding a single female flower and several male flowers, often with a yellow gland on its rim.

Cyathia go through the same cycle on every plant. They start out tight and green or red-tipped, open to shed yellow pollen, and then drop off. After the cyathia fall, the colored bracts usually follow before long.

It has been revealed that some of the newer poinsettia varieties hang on to their cyathia longer. So it isn't a sure thing, but it's still one of the better clues you get in the store. Any color works for this check, whether you're eyeing red or the pink poinsettias at Walmart (which come in a four-pack for maximum festive joy).

Bend down and look closely at the center of a few bracts. Plants on the same table can be at different stages, so check more than one. Ideally, the cyathia are mostly closed, green or tipped with red, and fresh-looking. Some yellow showing is fine on its own. That's often just the gland on the side of the cup – it doesn't mean the flower has opened.

Recent findings suggest that now compare that to a plant where the buds have split open and yellow pollen is dusting the bracts below them. If you see that, or you find bare stubs where cyathia used to be, that poinsettia has been blooming a while already. It may look fine today, but it has less time left than the one beside it with tight buds.

Classic red poinsettias come in a four-pack from Costa Farms, and you can order them on Amazon – and the same quick look at the center works on a plant that highlights up at the door.

According to recent reports, the green leaves under the bracts deserve a look too. Check for yellow leaves low on the stems, or bare spots where leaves have already dropped. Cold, poor light, and watering trouble can all cause that. Pass on a plant that droops or looks wilted, along with any that have torn, bruised, or creased bracts. Bluish or whitish edges on the bracts can be a sign of cold injury.

Recent findings suggest that flip a few leaves over as well. Whiteflies, such as the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), are common on poinsettias, and a puff of tiny white insects lifting off when you brush the plant is a bad sign.

Lift the pot if you can. Soggy soil in a heavy pot may mean it's been sitting in water inside its foil, and roots kept that wet can rot. Pay attention to where the plants are displayed, too. Poinsettias crowded by the automatic doors can catch a blast of cold air every time the doors open, and plants left packed in plastic sleeves for days can droop and drop their flowers early – ethylene gas builds up inside the sleeve.

When you get home, use a soil moisture meter, like the Xlux moisture meter available on Amazon, to take the guesswork out of watering.

Industry observers note that the journey home is where poinsettias tend to get hurt. When it's below 50°F (10°C) outside, sleeve or wrap the plant before it leaves the store, even for the short walk to the car. Just a few minutes of cold air can damage the bracts and leaves, and the damage may not show right away. Save the garden center for your last stop so the plant isn't stuck in a cold car while you're in other stores, and warm the car up first. Once you're inside, get the sleeve off pretty swiftly.

Recent findings suggest that pick a bright room for your poinsettia. Keep the plant near a window but out of hard, direct sun, and well clear of heat vents, the fireplace, and any door that lets in a draft.

According to recent reports, normal house temperatures work fine, roughly 65 to 70°F (18 to 21°C) during the day, with nights around 60°F (16°C) or a little warmer. Window glass gets cold at night, though, and so can the air right beside it. Set a digital indoor thermometer, like the TempPro TP50, for a night or two, and you'll know for sure.

Sources indicate that stick a finger in the pot before you water. If the top of the soil is dry, go ahead, and if it's still damp, wait a day or so. That shiny foil holds water like a bowl, so poke a few holes in the bottom, or take the pot out and water it over the sink until it drains. A ceramic planter, like this Garden & Home Red 8 Inch Indoor Ceramic Plant Pot, with drainage holes and saucer, is a much nicer option than foil anyway. You don't need fertilizer while a poinsettia is in bloom.

Recent findings suggest that pick a plant with tight little buds in the center, keep it somewhere warm and bright, and the color can hold for weeks after the holidays. So the next time you're standing in front of a whole table of red, skip past the brightest one for a second and look at the center first.

Industry News: Think Winter Kills All the Wasps in Your Yard? Here's Where Next Year's Queens Are Hiding

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After the first hard frost, the wasps that pestered every picnic in August are suddenly gone.
  • Before you look up how to kill wasps next spring, know that yellowjackets, paper wasps, and hornets live in colonies that last just one season.
  • It has been revealed that some of the places where wasps hide in winter are right in your yard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After the first hard frost, the wasps that pestered every picnic in August are suddenly gone. It's easy to figure the cold finished them off. So where do wasps go in winter, and do wasps die in winter at all? Most of them do – just not the ones that count for next year.

Before you look up how to kill wasps next spring, know that yellowjackets, paper wasps, and hornets live in colonies that last just one season. Each colony leaves behind young queens that have already mated and will ride out the cold on their own.

It has been revealed that some of the places where wasps hide in winter are right in your yard. Firewood, loose bark, and the gaps around a shed door can each hold a queen until spring.

Recent findings suggest that for the common social wasps, the colony only lasts a year. Each spring, a single queen starts a small nest and raises the first workers herself. The colony grows through summer, and by late summer it switches to raising males and fresh queens. The new queens mate in fall, then leave the nest for good.

Everyone else is left behind. By the time hard freezes settle in, the old queen, the workers, and the males have died, and the papery nest sits empty for good. The mated queens are the only ones that make it into winter, and they don't go back to the nest. Each one finds its own sheltered spot. Many still won't last until spring, but the ones that do will start the whole thing over.

Here are some of the common places you'll find queens hiding.

Sources indicate that rake back a deep drift of oak leaves in midwinter, and the ground underneath is often softer and less frozen than the open lawn. Yellowjacket queens may crawl into that leaf litter or under old mulch and pulled plants at the edge of a bed. They stay perfectly still. You'd likely never notice one. Some leaves left in place also help butterflies and moths overwinter, and there's no reason to rake every corner bare because of wasps.

Stacked firewood is full of narrow gaps out of the wind, and rotting logs and old stumps offer soft wood a queen can tuck into. Pull a few splits from the bottom of the stack in winter, and you may find one clinging to the bark, too cold to move much. Check each piece before carrying it inside – a warm living room can wake a dormant queen. Bring in only what you'll burn that day. Walmart's leather palm work gloves are tough enough for sorting through the stack.

Loose bark on a dead tree makes a snug pocket. Yellowjacket queens squeeze into those gaps. Birds have a hard time reaching them there, and the bark keeps off most of the weather. On a mild winter day, try lifting a slab of it off an old stump. You could find a queen pressed flat in the gap underneath, barely moving. Put the bark back if you do. She isn't going anywhere until spring.

Recent findings suggest that sheds, garages, and barns are full of cracks around door frames and window trim. Queens often move in during fall and stay put until spring. Paper wasps tend to seek out high spots for the winter, and they sometimes overwinter in clusters, packed together at the peak of a roof or along a rafter. To keep queens from slipping in next fall, cover open vents with stainless steel mesh, which Amazon sells in small sheets.

In a recent development, queens find their way into wall voids and attics through gaps where siding meets trim, or through cracks around windows. Temperatures in there usually stay above freezing. Ever find a slow, groggy wasp on a window inside the house in January? It's usually a lone queen that wandered in from the walls, drawn toward the light. An active nest looks different – steady traffic in and out of the same hole in summer or early fall points to a live colony inside the wall.

Industry observers note that don't plug that hole while the nest is active, since the wasps may chew through to the inside. Once the colony has died off, seal exterior cracks with a flexible sealant such as DAP Dynaflex 230 from Home Depot.

Industry observers note that some yellowjacket queens spend the winter underground, but not in the nest they came from. That old nest is abandoned when the colony dies, and it isn't used again. She might use an empty mouse or vole burrow instead, a crack between rocks, or a small pocket in loose soil.

In a recent development, A home compost pile that hasn't been turned in a while is another possibility. If you turn the pile in winter, move slowly and wear gloves, and she'll probably stay put.

In a recent development, usually, there's no need. Wasps are useful predators. Yellowjackets and paper wasps hunt caterpillars and other soft-bodied insects to feed their young, and the adults visit flowers for nectar, moving some pollen around as they go. A queen sleeping under a log at the back of the yard poses little risk, and next summer her colony will probably eat a good number of garden pests.

Doors, windows, and play areas are a different story. Seal gaps around the house in late summer, before queens go looking for winter shelter, and check that window screens fit tightly. Home Depot carries a door jamb weatherstrip set that closes the gaps around exterior doors.

According to recent reports, once spring warms up, glance at the eaves and porch ceiling every so often. A brand-newly introduced nest is about the size of a golf ball, and only the queen is tending it, so it's far easier to handle than a full colony in August. Large nests, ground nests, and anyone in the house who's allergic to stings are a job for a pest control professional.

In winter, the yard looks empty, but not entirely. Somewhere under those leaves or behind that bark, next year's wasps are sitting out the cold. Unless one is tucked in beside the back door, it can stay right where it is.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1452 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dogster

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that dogster is reader-supported.
  • Sources indicate that for families who have just lost a beloved pet, arranging cremation is often one of the last acts of love they can offer.
  • Sadly, for hundreds of families in the Philippines, that trust has been destroyed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

Sources indicate that for families who have just lost a beloved pet, arranging cremation is often one of the last acts of love they can offer. They choose a service, pay for the arrangements, and believe that their companion will be treated with dignity and respect. They may never see what happens behind the crematorium doors, but they trust that their furry family member is in caring hands.

Sadly, for hundreds of families in the Philippines, that trust has been destroyed.

What began as a neighborhood concern over a foul smell quickly turned into a disturbing discovery. On October 29, 2026, residents of Barangay Minuyan in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan, were disturbed by a strong, suffocating, and foul odor coming from a nearby vacant lot. The terrible stink prompted a report and closer inspection, leading to the nightmare-worthy discovery of seven large sacks containing the remains of 26 dogs and three cats; each one wrapped in plastic bags bearing identification labels with their names and weights.

The investigation eventually led to Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite, where many families had entrusted their deceased pets for cremation.

By November 4, authorities had recovered 29 animal carcasses, while 20 containers of ashes surrendered by families were undergoing forensic examination. The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is investigating possible fraud and other violations, and at least 250 pet owners have reportedly filed complaints against the company.

In a recent development, the questions are heartbreaking. Were these families given the ashes of their own pets? Were some animals never cremated at all? How did companions entrusted to a professional aftercare service end up in plastic bags beside a road?

For grieving pet owners, discovering that their furry family member's final arrangements may have been mishandled is an especially cruel betrayal.

Recent findings suggest that sadly, this is not the only case, or the only country, where fraud and deception have pervaded what should be a sacred service. In 2025, the Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Quintana Roo, Mexico, exposed a similarly disturbing situation. Authorities investigating a Chetumal pet crematorium found that families had paid to have their beloved companions cremated, only to receive urns containing soil instead of their pets' ashes. Even worse, more than 180 animal carcasses were reportedly discovered during searches connected with the investigation. The case involved allegations of fraud and improper disposal of animal remains, with legal proceedings continuing into 2026.

Different countries, different businesses, but an eerily similar betrayal. And in both cases, the damage potentially reaches far beyond the families who were deceived.

Another disturbing side of these horrific stories is the environmental impact. Improperly discarded animal remains can create environmental hazards, particularly when several carcasses accumulate in unmanaged locations.

As tissues decompose, bodily fluids and organic material are released. These substances can contribute to leachate, a liquid that may move through soil with rainfall and drainage. Depending on soil conditions, groundwater depth, and proximity to wells or waterways, this can create pathways for environmental contamination.

Biohazardous runoff, odors, and potential groundwater pollution are among the concerns associated with improperly managed animal carcasses. If investigators discover that remains were repeatedly discarded at multiple locations, removing the visible carcasses may not be enough. Surrounding soil, drainage systems, and nearby water sources may also need assessment.

The deceived pet owners deserve justice, but residents also need answers about the conditions around their homes.

According to recent reports, exposed animal remains can attract scavengers, including free-roaming dogs, cats, and wildlife. Insects may also come into contact with decomposing material and potentially spread infectious agents between locations.

Not every deceased animal carries an infectious disease, and finding carcasses does not automatically mean disease will spread. However, when the cause of death is unknown, there may be no way to determine whether the remains contain infectious agents that could expose other animals.

There is another potential hazard that pet owners may not immediately consider: euthanasia medications.

Pentobarbital, commonly used for humane euthanasia in veterinary medicine, can remain in an animal's tissues after death. Wildlife that consumes the remains of an animal euthanized with this drug can suffer secondary poisoning, with scavenging birds being particularly vulnerable.

And this is where the consequences can extend much further. Scavengers play an essential role in maintaining healthy ecosystems by removing animal carcasses before they become sources of environmental contamination and disease transmission. Vultures, for example, can consume remains that might otherwise attract other scavengers or allow infectious agents to persist in the environment. When scavenger populations decline, carcasses can remain accessible for longer, potentially increasing opportunities for pathogen transmission and disease spread.

It has been revealed that A carcass that should have been cremated could therefore become a source of danger to another animal. The irony is that the very animals helping keep ecosystems clean could be exposed to a potentially lethal drug simply because someone failed to dispose of a pet's remains responsibly.

Recent findings suggest that the scandals also raise questions about oversight of the pet aftercare industry. A business permit cannot demonstrate that every animal entrusted to a facility has been handled properly.

Families should be able to expect accountability throughout the process, from collection and identification to transportation, cremation, and the return of ashes. Records should establish which animal was received, where it was taken, and what happened to its remains.

The Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) notes the case has also highlighted a potential legal gap. According to the organization, the alleged deception may not fall directly under the Animal Welfare Act because the animals were already deceased when entrusted to the crematorium. However, the alleged conduct may constitute âestafaâ, or fraud by deceit, under the Revised Penal Code.

Affected families have been encouraged to preserve receipts, cremation certificates, photographs, messages, and other documentation that could support their complaints.

Sources indicate that the Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Mexico revealed a similarly disturbing situation, with more than 180 animal carcasses reportedly discovered and families allegedly receiving urns filled with soil instead of their pets' ashes. Two countries, two scandals, and far too many grieving families betrayed by businesses they trusted.

The death of a beloved pet is already a difficult time. Families make end-of-life decisions, discuss euthanasia with their veterinarians, arrange transportation, and decide how they would like to remember their companions.

According to recent reports, for some, receiving an urn containing their pet's ashes brings comfort. It becomes something tangible to keep beside a favorite photograph or in a special place at home. And while emotional cost is the most painful aspect for the affected pet owners, itâs also worth noting that individual cremation usually comes at a premium price; a price paid for a service not performed. But regardless of whether these pets were to have undergone individual or commingled cremation, families deserve honesty about the service they purchase.

They should never have to question whether the ashes they brought home belong to their furry family member.

There is something particularly upsetting about the possibility that an animal cherished throughout life, treated as family, and surrounded by affection could have its remains handled so carelessly.

People entrust pet aftercare providers with something deeply personal. They are saying goodbye to someone they loved. That deserves respect.

Breaking: Shea McGee Put Hydrangeas on Her Christmas Tree. Here’s How to Steal the Look

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hydrangeas really have their moment during the summer months, and then spend the winter looking dead, brown, and crispy while we politely look away.
  • According to recent reports, that's right, folks; not only did the Netflix Dream Home Makeover star give her hydrangeas some attention in winter, but she also added them to the star of the show during the holidays: her Christmas tree!
  • Recent findings suggest that as you may or may not know, Shea grows Limelight hydrangeas at her Salt Lake City home, telling fans that the blooms “bring me so much joy in the summer”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hydrangeas really have their moment during the summer months, and then spend the winter looking dead, brown, and crispy while we politely look away. Shea McGee, however, has made a point of doing the opposite, and to beautiful effect!

According to recent reports, that's right, folks; not only did the Netflix Dream Home Makeover star give her hydrangeas some attention in winter, but she also added them to the star of the show during the holidays: her Christmas tree! And, much like Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, it's one of those oh-so-simple but oh-so-effective ideas that we can't believe we didn't think of first.

Recent findings suggest that as you may or may not know, Shea grows Limelight hydrangeas at her Salt Lake City home, telling fans that the blooms “bring me so much joy in the summer”. Is it any wonder, then, that when the interior designer shared a video of her Christmas decor to Instagram, the blooms were front and center?

Industry observers note that A post shared by McGee & Co. (@mcgeeandco).

As you can see above, Shea McGee has decorated her tree with warm brown, tan, and cream ornaments, dried orange slices, clip-on LED candlesticks, and dried hydrangeas from her own garden (although you can buy ready-to-go cone hydrangeas from McGee & Co if you prefer an easier life).

According to recent reports, it's a beyond brilliant idea, as it means the blooms get a second act, which is a better return than most shrubs give you. If you want a similar look, just read on for some tips from the experts.

Shop Shea McGee-Inspired Christmas Decor:.

Keen to give it a whirl from scratch? Look this way...

Sources indicate that cameron of DreamHowYouLive favors Limelight (the same as Shea McGee grows) and Annabelle for a hydrangea arrangement. “Their petals dry stiff and papery, so they keep their shape, where softer mopheads crumble.”.

According to recent reports, flower farmer-florist Joey McFarland of Flowers by Dr. Jo agrees that panicle types like Limelight are best for long stems. He warns that bigleaf hydrangeas set buds in fall, so cutting too deeply means “cutting off your blooms for next year.” Shopping for plants? Browse our list of panicle hydrangea varieties.

Timing is highly notable as well, especially when it comes to hydrangeas. Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home waits until the heads “turn papery and antique in early fall.” Cut too soon and, as Cameron warns, “they wilt instead of drying.” (Which means you need to show patience, grasshopper).

When it comes to drying hydrangeas the experts all have a different opinion, which tells you how difficult it can actually be. Floral preservation artist Nadi Melam of Florals Memories says, “I always dry hydrangeas in a vase of water,” about an inch, for a “lovely muted antique color.”.

Cameron hangs them upside down in a dark, dry spot for two or three weeks, since vase-dried heads “tend to droop.” Our guide to drying hydrangea flowers covers both.

In a recent development, the best rule to follow if you want the Shea McGee effect? Water-drying holds shape and color well, while air-drying is quicker but leaves blooms more fragile.

There’s one place where most people go wrong when drying hydrangeas for Shea McGee-style decor. As Cameron tells me me he cuts the head town to 3-inch stems, wires each branch and tucks the whole bloom into a gap. His personal rule: “Three small clusters spread around the tree look intentional. One substantial bunch at the top looks like a mistake.”.

Arslan Ali of DecoroDea advises, “Treat them like picks, not ornaments,” and says to place them last, “after the ornaments and lights are already on,” so you fill the gaps that are actually still dark. Brooks wires clusters low near the trunk first, then moves smaller heads toward the tips. In essence, you can take a bit from every expert tip.

For McGee’s look, add dried orange slices, cream and tan ornaments, and warm white lights. Bright white, Cameron notes, makes “the whole thing look cold.”.

Dried petals shed, which is why Melam is so blunt with their advice: “You lose petals every time you touch a flower.” Cameron’s fix is a light hairspray mist that “keeps the shedding down.” And, as for those annoying relatives, who “just want to adjust one thing,” tell them that your Shea McGee-inspired Christmas tree is now a museum exhibit, so hands off".

According to recent reports, if you don't have real hydrangeas in your yard, faux hydrangeas as a no-mess alternative. These cream-white stems give the same soft look without the shedding.

Hydrangeas are also toxic if chewed, so keep clusters out of reach of curious pets.

Those candles on Shea McGee’s Christmas tree? Make them LED.

Melam indicates, “Open flame is a no-no since the dry material will ignite right away.” As for saving them for next year, the experts are once again split.

Want a warm glow like MsGee's but without the fire risk? These warm white, dimmable clip-on LED candles come with a remote, so you can keep real flames far from your dried hydrangeas.

Melam stores heads flat in a box with tissue between layers, and Cameron has reused the same heads two years running. However, McFarland indicates dried blooms “won’t do particularly well in storage” and suggests composting them and cutting fresh ones.

Either way, it’s a good excuse to plant more hydrangeas and see what tip works best for you.

#113921. What Your Snake Plant Needs in November – 5 Winter Care Checks to Keep It Glossy and Thriving

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1150 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

What Your Snake Plant Needs in November – 5 Winter Care Checks to Keep It Glossy and Thriving

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say.
  • Good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right.
  • Take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say. But that changes in November. The days get short, and the heat comes on, and the watering habit you kept all summer now leaves the potting mix wet for weeks. Yellow leaves and soft, mushy bases tend to follow.

Good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right. Once light levels drop, your snake plant isn't growing much, so it uses far less water and needs no fertilizer at all. What it does need is a dry pot between drinks, steady room temperatures, and a spot out of the cold air that pools along windows.

Take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks. Run through them now, then again on a gray afternoon in December. That alone considerably cuts the odds of losing a snake plant to winter.

Industry observers note that don't rely on a calendar when watering snake plants. A snake plant that needed water every two weeks in July might go a month or more between drinks in November. Its surface won't tell you much. So how do you know when it's dry? Push a finger down as far as it goes, or try the chopstick trick: push a wooden skewer to the bottom of the pot and pull it out. Damp mix clings to the wood and darkens it; dry mix leaves it clean.

If you're struggling to know when to water, then use a moisture meter for an accurate assessment, like the Xlux instant read probe, available from Amazon. Water only when the whole depth comes up dry, then let the pot drain fully. Leaves that go soft or flop over at the soil line usually mean the roots have sat wet too long.

In a recent development, low light is something a snake plant tolerates, not something it grows well in. In November, the sun sits lower and the days are short, so a dim corner that was fine in June may now get very little light. Growth slows, and the mix stays wet far longer because the plant is barely drawing water.

A spot within a few feet (about a meter) of an east or west window helps. Make the move gradual, though – a plant that goes straight from a dim hallway into hours of direct south sun can scorch.

Without a bright window, a grow light like the Sansi Pot-Clip-On Grow Light, positioned a foot or so (30 cm) above the leaves, fills the gap.

It has been revealed that on a cold evening, hold the back of your hand near the window where your snake plant sits. Chilly on your skin means chilly on the leaves, too. Blame single-pane glass, the gap under an outside door, or a nearby heating vent. Any of them can swing the temperature more than a snake plant can take – even while the thermostat reads fine.

Ordinary room temperatures are what you're after, roughly 60–85°F (16–29°C). Trouble starts if the plant sits below about 50°F (10°C) for long stretches. Leaves pressed against cold glass can develop soft, water-soaked patches. So at night, pull the pot back a foot or two (30–60cm) from the window.

If you want to see what the plant goes through after dark, then use a high/low thermometer, like the TempPro digital indoor thermometer, which displays both high and low temperature and humidity levels.

Industry observers note that tip the pot and look underneath. Drainage holes get plugged with compacted mix, a stray pebble, or roots that have grown through. In a decorative cachepot, a snake plant can stand in an inch (2.5 cm) of old water without anyone noticing. Lift it out and check. If the mix is still wet a week or more after you watered, it may have broken down and is holding too much moisture.

Sources indicate that winter is a poor time to disturb roots, so repotting snake plants is normally a spring job. The exception is a pot that won't drain at all – or a mix that stays soggy no matter what. Then a careful repot now beats rotting roots in March. For a replacement, choose a pot with a drainage hole and its own saucer, like this Vigoro ceramic planter from Home Depot. Fill it with a gritty potting mix, like Miracle-Gro Cactus, Palm, and Citrus Mix, which drains much faster than regular potting soil.

Look each leaf over, down to the soil line, for signs of common snake plant problems. If yellow is creeping up from the base and the leaf feels soft or mushy there, you're looking at overwatering and rotting roots. Cold damage can look a lot like it, though. Wrinkled or curling leaves usually mean the reverse: the plant went too long between drinks.

Next, check the crevices where leaves overlap for pests. Cottony white tufts there are mealybugs (Planococcus citri), and small tan or brown bumps that stay put when nudged are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

In a recent development, dab a few with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, then follow up with a ready-to-use insecticidal soap, like Garden Safe insecticidal soap, sprayed right onto the insects. It's far easier to deal with a dozen now than hundreds in February.

Put the fertilizer away until spring. A plant that isn't actively growing can't use the feed, so unused salts build up in the mix and can burn roots. Hold off on routine repotting for the same reason. Fresh mix and a bigger pot push a plant toward newly introduced growth right when the light to support it is lowest. Disturbed roots also recover slowly in a cool room.

Industry observers note that don't water your snake plant on a schedule just because the heat is drying out the air. Dry air and dry soil aren't the same thing, and a snake plant copes with dry air far better than it does with wet roots. For the next few months, you want it holding steady, not growing.

Run the same five checks again around the new year. In winter, a snake plant mostly needs the right spot and to be left alone. Give it that, and the one looking a bit tired in November is usually putting up new leaves by late spring.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.
